p.seg: First [Section on] Ministering to Lu
Kǒngzǐ, in his first official position,
was made magistrate of Zhōngdū.
He established regulations for supporting the living and burying the dead.
The old and young ate differently,
the strong and weak had different duties,
men and women walked on separate paths;
lost items were not picked up on the road,
utensils were not carved with false decorations;
coffins were made of four cùn wood,
outer coffins of five cùn wood,
tombs followed the shape of hills,
without mounds or trees.
After a year of implementing these,
the feudal lords of the west imitated them.
Duke Dìng said to Kǒngzǐ,
"If your method is learned,
what will become of the state of Lǔ?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"Even the whole world would be manageable!
Why only the state of Lǔ?"
Therefore, after two years,
Duke Dìng appointed him Minister of Works.
Thereupon, he distinguished the natures of the five types of soil,
so that things each obtained the appropriate place for their growth,
and all found their proper place.
Previously,
the Jì family buried Duke Zhāo south of the tomb path;
Kǒngzǐ dug a ditch and connected all the tombs,
saying to Jì Huánzǐ,
"You are belittling the ruler to publicize your own offense.
fēi lǐ yě. is not proper etiquette.
Jīn hé zhī, Now connecting them,
suǒ yǐ yǎn fūzǐ zhī bù chén." is in order to conceal the fact that the masters are not loyal subjects."
Yóu sīkōng wèi Lǔ dà sī kòu, He served as Minister of Works, then as Grand Minister of Justice for Lǔ,
shè fǎ ér bù yòng, established laws which were not even needed,
wú jiān mín. and there were no deceitful people.
Dìng Gōng yǔ Qí hóu huì yú Jiágǔ. Duke Dìng met with the Marquis of Qí at Jiágǔ.
Kǒngzǐ shè xiàng shì, Kǒngzǐ acted as the master of ceremonies,
yuē: and said:
"chén wén yǒu wén shì zhě bì yǒu wǔ bèi, "Your servant has heard that those engaged in civil affairs must have military preparations,
yǒu wǔ shì zhě bì yǒu wén bèi. and those engaged in military affairs must have civil preparations.
Gǔ zhě zhū hóu bìng chū jiāng, In ancient times when feudal lords went beyond their borders together,
bì jù guān yǐ cóng, they would certainly bring a full complement of officials with them,
qǐng jù zuǒ yòu sīmǎ." I request to bring the left and right commanders."
Dìng Gōng cóng zhī. Duke Dìng followed his advice.
Zhì huì suǒ, Arriving at the meeting place,
wèi tán, they built an altar
tǔ jiē sān děng, with three levels of earthen steps,
yǐ yù lǐ xiāng jiàn, in order to meet each other with proper ceremony,
yī ràng ér dēng. bowing and yielding as they ascended.
After the presentation of ceremonial wine was complete,
the envoy from Qí 齊, a man from Lái 萊, used soldiers and drums to create a disturbance,
threatening Dìng Gōng 定公.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 went up the steps and advanced,
urging the duke to withdraw.
He said:
"Gentlemen,
they are using weapons against him.
Our two lords are seeking amity,
these captives from distant barbarian tribes,
dare to disrupt it with weapons;
this is not how the lord of Qí 齊 commands the feudal lords.
Barbarians do not plot against the civilized,
foreigners do not disturb the Chinese,
captives do not interfere with covenants,
weapons do not coerce friendship.
To the spirits, it is inauspicious;
to virtue, it is a transgression of righteousness;
to people, it is a loss of propriety.
Your lord must not allow this."
The lord of Qí 齊 felt ashamed in his heart,
and waved them away to avoid the situation.
After a while,
Qí 齊 began to perform palace music,
and actors and dwarfs performed in front.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 quickly stepped forward,
ascending the steps,
not completing a single level.
Said:
"A commoner who deceives and insults the feudal lords
deserves to be punished.
I request the Right Sīmǎ to quickly carry out the execution."
Thereupon, he executed the dwarf,
dismembering his body.
The Marquis of Qí was afraid
and appeared ashamed.
As they were about to make an alliance,
the people of Qí added to the written oath, saying:
"If the Qí army goes beyond the border
and does not follow me with three hundred chariots,
may this alliance be like this."
Kǒngzǐ instructed Zī Wúhuán to reply:
"If you do not return the fields of Wènyáng to us,
which we used to fulfill our obligations,
then it will be the same for us."
The Marquis of Qí was about to set up a banquet,
and Kǒngzǐ said to Liángqiū Jù:
"How could you not have heard about the past relations between Qí and Lǔ?
To offer a banquet after the matter is already settled is to trouble the officials.
Furthermore, sacrificial oxen and ivory objects should not leave the temple,
and joyous music should not be performed in the open fields.
To offer a banquet when everything is already prepared
is to abandon propriety.
If it is not fully prepared,
This is using inferior rice.
Using inferior rice is a disgrace to the lord;
Abandoning propriety brings a bad name.
Why don't you consider this?
Now, the offering is a means of displaying virtue.
If it doesn't display virtue,
it's better to have not done it at all."
Consequently, he did not proceed with the offering.
When the Marquis of Qí 齊侯 returned,
he rebuked his ministers, saying:
"Lǔ 魯 uses the way of the superior man to assist its lord,
but you alone use the way of barbarians to instruct me,
causing me to commit offenses."
Thereupon, he returned the four towns he had seized from Lǔ 魯, as well as the fields of Wèn Yáng 汶陽.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said to Duke Dìng 定公:
"A household should not store armor,
and a town should not have walls of a hundred *zhì* (3 *zhàng* tall),
according to the ancient regulations.
Now, the Three Families exceed these regulations.
I request that they all be reduced."
Thereupon, he ordered Zhòng Yóu 仲由, the steward of the Jì 季 family, to demolish the three cities.
Shūsūn 叔孫 was displeased with the Jì 季 family.
Because of this, he used Gōngshān Fúráo 公山弗擾, the steward of Fèi 費,
to lead the people of Fèi 費 in an attack on Lǔ 魯.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子, along with Duke Dìng 定公, Jìsūn 季孫, Zhòngsūn 仲孫, and Shūsūn 叔孫,
entered the palace of the Fèi 費 family
Climbing the Terrace of Wǔzǐ.
The people of Fèi attacked it,
reaching the side of the terrace.
Kǒngzǐ ordered Shēn Jūxū and Yuè Qí
to rally the troops,
and descend to attack them.
The people of Fèi were defeated and fled north.
Consequently, he destroyed the walls of the three capitals,
strengthened the ducal house,
weakened the private families,
honored the ruler and humbled the ministers,
and political transformation greatly progressed.
Initially,
in Lǔ, there was a sheep merchant named Shěn Yóushì,
who would regularly give his sheep water in the morning to deceive the market people;
there was a Gōng Shènshì
whose wife was promiscuous and uncontrollable;
there was a Shèn Kuìshì
whose extravagance exceeded the law;
in Lǔ, those who sold livestock
would embellish them to inflate the price.
When Kǒngzǐ took office,
Shěn Yóushì dared not give his sheep water in the morning;
Gōng Shènshì divorced his wife;
Shèn Kuìshì crossed the border and moved away.
After three months,
Then those who sell cattle and horses do not hoard prices;
those who sell piglets do not add adornments;
men and women walking separate their paths;
people do not pick up lost items on the road;
men value loyalty and trustworthiness,
women value chastity and obedience;
visitors from all directions who arrive in the town,
do not seek out the officials,
all feel as if they have returned home.
The Beginning of Execution, Section Two
Kǒngzǐ became the Minister of Justice of Lǔ,
acting as prime minister,
and had a joyous expression.
Zhòng Yóu asked,
"Yóu has heard that the virtuous man does not fear the arrival of misfortune,
and does not rejoice at the arrival of good fortune.
Now, Master, you have gained position and are joyful,
why is this?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Indeed!
There is such a saying.
Does it not say to rejoice in valuing those beneath you?"
Thereupon, after governing the court for seven days, he executed the rebellious official Shào Zhèng Mǎo,
executing him beneath the two watchtowers,
displaying his corpse in the court for three days.
Zǐgòng stepped forward and said,
“Now, Shào Zhèng Mǎo was a famous man of Lǔ.
Now that you, Master, are in power and have begun to execute him,
perhaps this is a mistake?”
Confucius said:
“Sit down!
I will tell you the reason for this.
There are five great evils in the world,
and theft is not among them.
The first is being inwardly rebellious and treacherous,
the second is behaving perversely and stubbornly,
the third is speaking falsely and eloquently,
the fourth is remembering shameful things and being knowledgeable,
the fifth is conforming to what is wrong and being ingratiating.
If a person has any one of these five,
then he cannot escape the punishment of a junzi,
zé bùmiǎn jūnzǐ zhī zhū,
and Shào Zhèng Mǎo possesses them all.
His residence is sufficient to gather followers and form a party,
his speeches are sufficient to adorn praises and deceive the masses,
his strength and resistance are sufficient to oppose what is right and stand alone;
this is a treacherous leader of men,
and cannot be eliminated.
Now, Yīn Tāng executed Yǐn Xié,
King Wén executed Pān Zhèng,
Duke Zhōu executed Guǎn Cài,
Grand Duke executed Huá Shì,
Guǎn Zhòng executed Fù Yǐ,
Zǐ Chǎn executed Shǐ Hé,
All these seven men, though living in different eras, were similarly put to death.
It is because these seven men, though living in different eras, shared the same wickedness,
that they could not be pardoned.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"My heart is heavy with sorrow,
I am angered by the multitude of petty men."
When petty men form a group,
it is indeed a cause for worry."
Kǒngzǐ was the Grand Minister of Justice of Lǔ.
There was a father and son who were in litigation.
The Master had them both arrested and imprisoned together.
For three months, they were not separated.
The father requested that the case be dropped.
The Master then pardoned them.
Jìsūn heard of this
and was displeased.
He said:
"The Minister of Justice is deceiving me!
He previously told me:
'To govern a state, one must first begin with filial piety.'
I intended to execute a filial offender to teach the people about filial piety;
wouldn't that have been a good thing?
But now he has pardoned him.
Why is that?"
Rǎn Yǒu told Kǒngzǐ about this.
Kǒngzǐ sighed deeply and said:
"Wūhū!
For superiors to lose their way and kill their inferiors
is not reasonable.
To not teach them filial piety and then hear their cases
is to kill the innocent.
When the entire army is defeated,
they cannot all be executed.
When the prisons are not well-managed,
punishments cannot be carried out.
Why?
Because the superiors' teachings are not being followed,
the blame does not lie with the people.
To be lenient with orders but strict with punishments
is to be a thief.
To collect taxes without a set time
is to be oppressive.
To declare something a success without trying it out
is to be cruel.
Therefore, if these three are absent,
then punishment can be immediately applied.
The *Shū* [Book of Documents] says:
'Just punishments and just executions,
do not use them to satisfy your own heart,
but only say that there is no matter that has been carefully considered.'
This means one must first teach and then punish.
If one has already presented moral teachings in order to first subdue them,
and they are still not amenable,
then one should promote the worthy to encourage them.
If that is not acceptable,
then abolish it;
if that is still not acceptable,
only then use awe to intimidate them.
If this is done for three years, the people will be upright.
If there are wicked people who do not conform to the transformation,
then deal with them with punishment,
and the people will all know what is a crime.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
‘The Son of Heaven is the support,
causing the people not to be confused.’
Therefore, sternness is present but not tested,
punishments are laid aside and not used.
The present age is not like this;
it disrupts their teachings,
complicates their punishments,
causing the people to be confused and trapped by them,
and then controls them,
therefore, punishments become more numerous and thieves cannot be overcome.
Now, a three-foot barrier,
an empty cart cannot climb it,
why?
Because it is steep;
a hundred-cubit mountain,
a heavy load ascends it,
why?
Because the slope is gradual.
The gradual slope of the present world has been in place for a long time,
Even if there are penal laws,
can the people be prevented from transgressing?"
*Wáng Yán Jiě Dì Sān* (Third Section on Explaining Royal Words)
*Kǒngzǐ* was at leisure,
and *Zēng Shēn* was attending him.
*Kǒngzǐ* said,
"*Shēn*!
The gentlemen of today
only listen to the words of scholars and high officials.
As for the words of the true gentlemen,
they are rare.
Alas!
I speak of the royal words that, without leaving the door or window, transform the world."
*Zēngzǐ* rose,
descended from his mat, and replied,
"May I venture to ask what are the royal words?"
*Kǒngzǐ* did not answer.
*Zēngzǐ* said,
"It is difficult to attend the Master at leisure,
therefore I dare to ask."
*Kǒngzǐ* still did not answer.
*Zēngzǐ* became respectful and fearful,
hitched up his robe and withdrew,
stood with his mat on his back.
After a while,
*Kǒngzǐ* sighed,
turned and said to *Zēngzǐ*,
"Shēn!
You can be told the Way of the enlightened king."
Zēngzǐ said:
"I dare not consider myself sufficient,
but I would like to learn from what I have heard."
The Master said:
"Sit down,
I will tell you.
The Way,
is how to illuminate virtue;
virtue,
is how to venerate the Way.
Therefore, without virtue the Way is not venerated,
without the Way, virtue is not illuminated.
Even if one has fine horses of the state,
if they are not trained and ridden according to the proper way,
one cannot travel far;
even if one has vast lands and many people,
if they are not governed according to the proper way,
one cannot achieve hegemony.
Therefore,
in the past, the enlightened kings cultivated the Seven Teachings internally,
and practiced the Three Attainments externally.
When the Seven Teachings are cultivated,
then one can defend;
when the Three Attainments are practiced,
then one can conquer.
The way of the enlightened king,
in his defense,
surely deflects attacks from a thousand miles away;
in his conquests,
surely returns the army as if from resting on a mat.
Therefore it is said,
"Cultivate internally the seven teachings,
and the ruler above will not be weary;
enact externally the three reaches,
and wealth will not be wasted."
This is called the way of the enlightened king."
Zēngzǐ said:
"An enlightened king who is neither wearying nor wasteful,
may I be permitted to hear about it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the past,
Emperor Shùn had Yǔ on his left and Gāo Yáo on his right,
and without leaving his mat, the world was governed.
If it is like this,
how could the ruler above be weary?
If the governance is not centered,
it is the ruler's misfortune;
if the orders are not carried out,
it is the ministers' fault.
If the tax is only one-eleventh,
and the people's labor is used
for no more than three days a year;
and when entering the mountains and marshes, it is done in the proper season without levies;
and tolls at the passes, inspections at the markets, and shops in the city do not collect taxes.
These are the ways to generate wealth,
and the enlightened king economizes on these,
how then is wealth wasted?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I venture to ask what are the seven teachings?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If superiors respect the elderly,
then inferiors will be more filial;
if superiors honor age,
then inferiors will be more fraternal;
if superiors enjoy giving,
then inferiors will be more generous;
if superiors are close to the virtuous,
then inferiors will choose their friends wisely;
if superiors love virtue,
then inferiors will not conceal anything;
if superiors despise greed,
then inferiors will be ashamed to contend;
if superiors are upright and yield,
then inferiors will be ashamed to hoard.
These are called the Seven Teachings.
The Seven Teachings
are the foundation of governing the people.
When the teachings and governance are established,
then the foundation is upright.
All superiors
are examples for the people.
If the standard is upright, what will not be upright?
Therefore, a ruler should first establish benevolence within himself;
then the high officials will be loyal, and the scholars will be trustworthy,
the people will be honest and the customs simple,
men will be sincere and women chaste.
These six things are the result of instruction.
Spread them throughout the world and in every direction, and they will not be wanting;
apply them in ordinary homes, and they will not be obstructed.
Regulate them with ritual,
establish them with righteousness,
and implement them with obedience,
then the people's rejection of evil will be like pouring hot water on snow!"
Zēngzǐ said:
"The Way has reached its limit;
your disciple is not sufficient to make it clear."
Confucius said:
"Shēn, do you think that is all?
There is more.
In the past,
the enlightened kings had methods for governing the people;
they would certainly divide the land and enfeoff them,
and distribute responsibilities to govern them;
then virtuous people would have nowhere to hide,
and violent people would have nowhere to lie low.
They would order the officials to examine and evaluate them daily and periodically,
to promote and employ the virtuous and good,
and to demote and dismiss the unworthy.
If that is the case, then the worthy will be pleased, and the unworthy will be afraid,
Have compassion for widowers and widows,
provide for orphans and the childless,
relieve the poor,
encourage filial piety and brotherly love,
select the talented;
if these seven are cultivated,
then within the four seas there will be no criminals.
The ruler's affection for the people below
is like that of the hands and feet for the heart;
the people's affection for the ruler above
is like that of a young child for its loving mother.
When those above and those below are so affectionate towards each other,
then orders are followed,
commands are carried out,
the people cherish his virtue,
those near are pleased and submit,
those far away come and attach themselves;
this is the achievement of governance.
Now, by spreading the fingers, one knows the *cun* (inch);
by spreading the hand, one knows the *chi* (foot);
by extending the elbow, one knows the *xun* (fathom);
these are the principles of not being far off.
The Zhōu Dynasty system was such that,
three hundred paces made a *li* (里, approximately 0.5 km),
a thousand paces formed a *jing* (井, a unit of land division),
three *jing* made a *lie* (埒, an enclosure),
three *lie* made a *ju* (矩, a square),
fifty *li* made a *du* (都, a capital city),
To enfeoff a hundred li to establish a state;
is to accumulate stores and gather resources there.
To be concerned with whether travelers have what they need.
Therefore, the Mányí barbarians and all the Xià peoples,
although their clothing and headwear are different,
and their languages do not match,
none fail to come as guests.
Therefore it is said:
Without a market, the people are not lacking;
without punishments, the people are not disordered.
Hunting and fishing with nets,
is not to fill palaces and chambers;
levying taxes from the common people,
is not to fill treasuries and storehouses.
To feel compassion and distress to make up for deficiencies,
and use ritual restraint to lessen excess.
Believing in much and using few appearances,
such rituals can be upheld,
such words can be repeated,
such traces can be followed;
like eating when hungry,
like drinking when thirsty,
the people trust them,
like the inevitable verification of cold and heat.
Therefore, seeing the distant as near,
is not because the way is near,
but because of seeing bright virtue.
Therefore, weapons of war do not move, yet there is awe;
To employ benefits without bestowing them, yet be close to the people,
this is what is meant by the "guarding" of an enlightened ruler,
he who repels attacks from a thousand *lǐ* away."
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I venture to ask, what are the 'Three Perfections'?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Perfect propriety requires no concession, and the world is well-ordered;
Perfect reward requires no expenditure, and the scholars of the world are pleased;
Perfect music makes no sound, and the people of the world are harmonious.
An enlightened ruler diligently practices these Three Perfections,
therefore the rulers of the world can be known,
the scholars of the world can be made his subjects,
and the people of the world can be employed."
Zēngzǐ said:
"May I venture to ask, what is the meaning of this principle?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In ancient times, the enlightened rulers
were sure to know all the names of the good scholars in the world;
having known their names,
they also knew their substance,
and also knew their number and where they were located.
Then, based on the ranks of the world, they honored them;
this is what is meant by 'Perfect propriety requires no concession, and the world is well-ordered.'
Based on the emoluments of the world, they enriched the scholars of the world;
this is what is meant by 'Perfect reward requires no expenditure, and the scholars of the world are pleased.'
If it is like this,
then the reputation of the world will rise up,
this is what is meant by 'Perfect music makes no sound, and the people of the world are harmonious.'
故曰：
所謂天下之至仁者，
能合天下之至親也；
所謂天下之至明者，

能舉天下之至賢者也。 Therefore it is said: Those who are called the most benevolent in the world are able to unite those who are the most closely related in the world; those who are called the most discerning in the world are able to elevate those who are the most virtuous in the world.
此三者咸通，
然後可以征。 When these three things are all accomplished, then one can undertake a campaign.
是故仁者莫大乎愛人，
智者莫大乎知賢，

賢政者莫大乎官能。 Therefore, for the benevolent, nothing is greater than loving the people; for the wise, nothing is greater than knowing the virtuous; for virtuous governance, nothing is greater than employing the capable.
有土之君，
修此三者，
則四海之內，
共命而已矣。 A ruler who possesses territory, if he cultivates these three things, then within the four seas, (people) will only obey his commands.
夫明王之所征，
必道之所廢者也。 The campaigns of an enlightened king are necessarily directed towards those who have abandoned the Way.
是故誅其君而改其政，
弔其民而不奪其財。 Therefore, (he) punishes their ruler and reforms their government, consoles their people and does not seize their wealth.
故明王之政，
猶時雨之降，
降至則民說矣。 Therefore, the government of an enlightened king is like timely rain that descends; when it descends, the people are pleased.
是故行施彌博，
得親彌眾，

此之謂還師衽席之上。 」 Therefore, his acts of generosity are exceedingly extensive, and the number of those who become close to him is exceedingly numerous. This is what is meant by "returning the army on a mat and pillow."
大昏解第四 Chapter Four: Explanation of the Great Wedding
Kǒngzǐ shì zuò yú Āi Gōng. Kǒngzǐ was attending Āi Gōng (Duke Ai).
公曰：
「Gǎn wèn rén dào shú wèi dà? 」 "May I ask, in the way of humanity, what is the greatest?"
Kǒngzǐ qiǎo rán zuò sè ér duì yuē: Kǒngzǐ looked grave and replied:
「Jūn zhī jí cǐ yán yě, "That you, O lord, have raised this question,
bǎixìng zhī huì yě, is a blessing for the common people.
gù chén gǎn wú cí ér duì? Therefore, how could your subject dare not to answer?
Rén dào zhèng wèi dà. In the way of humanity, governance is the greatest.
Fú zhèng zhě, zhèng yě. Now, governance is rectification.
Jūn wèi zhèng, If the ruler is upright,
zé bǎixìng cóng ér zhèng yǐ. then the common people will follow and be upright.
Jūn zhī suǒ wèi, What the ruler does,
bǎixìng zhī suǒ cóng; is what the common people follow;
jūn bù wéi zhèng, if the ruler is not upright,
bǎixìng hé suǒ cóng hū? 」 what will the common people follow?"
Gōng yuē: The Duke said:
「Gǎn wèn wéi zhèng rú zhī hé? 」 "May I ask, what should governance be like?"
Kǒngzǐ duì yuē: Kǒngzǐ replied:
「Fūfù bié, "Husband and wife have their separate roles,
nánnǚ qīn, men and women are affectionate,
jūn chén xìn; ruler and subject are trustworthy;
sān zhě zhèng, If these three are rectified,
zé shù wù cóng zhī. 」 then all things will follow."
Gōng yuē: The Duke said:
「Guǎrén suī wú néng yě, "Although I, the寡人 (term used by dukes/kings to refer to themselves), am incompetent,
yuàn rú suǒyǐ xíng sān zhě zhī dào, I wish to know the way to implement these three,
kě dé wén hū? 」 may I be allowed to hear it?"
Kǒngzǐ duì yuē: Kǒngzǐ replied:
「Gǔ zhī wéi zhèng, "In ancient times, governance,
Loving people is paramount;
therefore, in governing the love of people,
ritual is paramount;
therefore, in governing ritual,
respect is paramount;
the utmost of respect
the great marriage is paramount;
the great marriage has arrived;
the great marriage having arrived,
wearing the crown and personally welcoming [the bride];
the personal welcoming [of the bride],
is respect.
Therefore, the gentleman cultivates respect as a means of being close to his relatives;
abandoning respect,
is to abandon one's relatives;
not being close nor respectful,
is not showing honor.
Love and respect,
are they not the foundation of governance?"
The Duke said:
"I wish to speak about this:
wearing the crown and personally welcoming [the bride],
is it not already too much of a burden?"
Kǒngzǐ solemnly changed his expression and replied,
"Combining the goodness of two surnames,
to continue the descendants of the former sages,
to establish the masters of the ancestral temples and altars of the realm,
what do you mean by 'too much of a burden'?"
The Duke said:
"I am indeed unenlightened.
If I were not unenlightened,
how could I have heard these words?
I desire to ask,
but I cannot find the words,
please elaborate a little."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If Heaven and Earth do not unite,
the myriad things will not be born;
the great marriage is the continuation of myriad generations,
why does Your Lordship consider it a burden?"
Kǒngzǐ then said:
"Internally, using them to regulate the rites of the ancestral temple is
sufficient to match the spirits of Heaven and Earth;
externally, using them to regulate the rites of forthright speech is
sufficient to establish respect between superiors and inferiors.
If things feel shame, it is sufficient to invigorate them;
if the state feels shame, it is sufficient to revive it.
Therefore, governing begins with rites;
rites, are they not the foundation of governance!"
Kǒngzǐ then said:
"In the past, the enlightened kings of the Three Dynasties certainly respected their wives and children,
there was a principle to it.
The wife,
is the progenitor of one's relatives;
the son,
(The body is) a legacy from one's parents,
how dare one not be reverent with it?
Therefore, a gentleman is always reverent.
To be reverent,
to be reverent towards one's body is of utmost importance;
the body,
is a branch from one's parents,
how dare one not be reverent with it?
To not be reverent towards one's body,
is to harm one's parents;
to harm one's parents,
is to harm one's root;
to harm one's root,
then the branches will follow it to ruin.
These three—themselves, their children, and their spouses—are models for the common people.
Taking care of themselves,
taking care of their children,
taking care of their spouses,
if the ruler can cultivate these three,
then great transformation will spread throughout the world.
In the past, the way of Dà Wáng was like this,
and the country was well-ordered."
Gōng said:
"May I ask, what does it mean to be reverent towards one's body?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"If a gentleman's words are excessive, the people will create sophistry;
if his actions are excessive, the people will create disorder.
If his words are not excessive,
If actions are not excessive,
the common people will respectfully obey orders.
If this is the case,
then it can be said that he is able to respect himself,
if he is able to respect himself,
then he is able to fulfill his familial responsibilities."
The Duke said:
"What does it mean to fulfill one's familial responsibilities?"
Confucius replied:
"A *jūnzǐ* is one who achieves a name.
The common people give him the name,
call him *jūnzǐ*,
and this is fulfilling the familial responsibilities, being a ruler and also acting as a son to the people."
Confucius then said:
"To govern and not be able to love the people,
then one cannot perfect oneself;
if one cannot perfect oneself,
then one cannot secure one's land;
if one cannot secure one's land,
then one cannot find joy in Heaven.
If one cannot find joy in Heaven,
then one cannot perfect oneself."
The Duke said:
"May I ask, what does it mean to be able to perfect oneself?"
Confucius replied:
"If one's conduct does not exceed what is proper,
this is called perfecting oneself;
not exceeding what is proper,
It accords with the Way of Heaven."
The Duke said:
"What does a gentleman value in the Way of Heaven?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He values its ceaselessness.
Like the sun and moon following each other from east to west without ceasing,
this is the Way of Heaven;
being open and able to endure,
this is the Way of Heaven;
accomplishing things without acting,
this is the Way of Heaven;
and illuminating what has already been accomplished,
this is the Way of Heaven."
The Duke said:
"I am but foolish and ignorant,
I am fortunate that you weary your mind with this."
Kǒngzǐ abruptly moved from his mat and replied:
"A benevolent person does not overstep things,
a filial son does not overstep his parents.
Therefore, a benevolent person serves his parents as he serves Heaven,
and serves Heaven as he serves his parents.
This is what is meant by a filial son completing himself."
The Duke said:
"Now that I have heard such words,
what should I do about subsequent faults?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"That Your Lordship reaches these words,
is the blessing of your minister."
Explanation of the Conduct of Scholars, Chapter Five
Kǒngzǐ was in Wèi.
Rǎn Qiú said to Jì Sūn,
"The state has a sage,
but cannot employ him.
Wanting to seek order by these means,
is like stepping backwards and wanting to catch up with the people ahead.
It cannot be achieved.
Now Kǒngzǐ is in Wèi,
and they are going to employ him.
To have talent ourselves and use it to benefit a neighboring state,
is difficult to call wise.
Please invite him with generous gifts."
Jì Sūn told Āi Gōng about this,
and the duke followed his advice.
Kǒngzǐ arrived,
and was housed in Āi Gōng's guesthouse.
The Duke ascended from the eastern steps,
Kǒngzǐ from the guest's steps,
and stood in attendance in the hall.
The Duke said,
"Master's attire,
is it the attire of a scholar?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"Qiū spent his youth in Lǔ,
wearing clothes with overlapping lapels;
and grew up in Sòng,
Wearing a crown and *zhāngfǔ* cap.
Qiū heard of it:
"The learning of a *jūnzǐ* is broad,
their clothing follows the customs of the local area.
Qiū doesn't know that this is *rú* clothing."
The Duke said:
"May I ask about *rú* conduct?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"To speak briefly,
one cannot exhaust their qualities;
to enumerate them in detail,
even if one were to keep adding servants, one could not adequately describe them."
Āi Gōng ordered mats to be arranged.
Kǒngzǐ sat in attendance,
and said:
"The *rú* possesses treasures on their mat, waiting to be employed;
they diligently study day and night, waiting to be questioned;
they cherish loyalty and trustworthiness, waiting to be recommended;
they exert themselves in practice, waiting to be selected;
their self-establishment is like this.
The *rú* is mindful in their clothing and cap,
cautious in their actions,
generous to the point of appearing negligent,
modest to the point of seeming disingenuous;
in great matters, they are like majesty,
in small matters, they are like shame;
they are difficult to draw forward but easy to withdraw,
they are diligent as if lacking ability;
Such is the countenance they possess.
The *rú* has difficulty finding a dwelling,
Their sitting and rising are respectful,
Their words are certainly sincere and trustworthy,
Their actions are certainly upright and just;
On the roads, they do not contend for advantages in dangerous or easy places,
In winter and summer, they do not contend for harmony of yin and yang;
They cherish their death in order to have something to await,
They nourish their bodies in order to have something to accomplish;
Such is the preparation they possess.
The *rú* does not treasure gold and jade;
But considers loyalty and trustworthiness as treasures;
Does not pray for land,
But considers benevolence and righteousness as land;
Does not seek to accumulate much,
But considers extensive learning as wealth;
They are difficult to obtain but easy to provide for,
Easy to provide for but difficult to keep;
They are not seen at improper times,
Is this not difficult to obtain?
They do not associate with those who are unrighteous,
Is this not difficult to keep?
They labor first and receive emolument later,
Is this not easy to provide for?
Such is their closeness to human feelings.
The *rú*, entrusted with goods and wealth, is not greedy,
Immersed in pleasurable pursuits, is not dissolute,
Threatened by a crowd, is not afraid,
He is not intimidated when opposed by soldiers;
Seeing profit, he does not compromise his righteousness;
Seeing death, he does not change his principles;
When fierce insects fight, he does not measure their courage;
When pulling a heavy tripod, he does not measure his strength;
He does not regret what has passed;
He does not anticipate what is to come;
He does not repeat rash words;
He does not dwell on rumors;
He does not sever his dignity;
He does not practice scheming;
Such is his independence.
The *rú* is approachable but not coercible,
can be near but not forced,
can be killed but not humiliated;
His dwelling is not extravagant;
His food is not rich;
His faults can be slightly debated but not openly rebuked;
Such is his firmness.
The *rú* has loyalty and trustworthiness as armor,
ritual and righteousness as shields and lances;
He goes out wearing benevolence,
and lives embracing righteousness;
Even if there is tyrannical rule,
he does not change his place;
Such is his self-reliance.
The *rú* has a one-mu palace,
a room surrounded by earthen walls,
A wattle gate with a round hole,
a tumbleweed door with earthenware jug windows,
changing clothes to go out,
eating only every other day;
if the ruler answers him,
he does not dare to doubt;
if the ruler does not answer,
he does not dare to flatter;
such is his service.
A Rú (Confucian scholar) lives like the people of today,
and examines the ancients,
puts it into practice in the present age,
and is taken as a model by later generations;
if he does not meet with the times,
not supported by those above,
not promoted by those below,
deceitful and flattering people,
will form factions and endanger him,
his person may be endangered,
but his will cannot be taken away;
even in danger,
his daily life still wholly trusts in his will,
and he does not forget the suffering of the common people;
such are his worries and thoughts.
A Rú has broad learning that is inexhaustible,
earnest practice that is tireless,
secluded living without lewdness,
communication with superiors without being stymied;
Ritual certainly emphasizes harmony,
acting leisurely within the bounds of the law,
admiring the worthy and accepting the multitude,
breaking off corners and joining like tiles;
such is their magnanimity.
The Rú (Confucian) internally praises without avoiding relatives,
externally recommends without avoiding grudges,
assesses accomplishments and accumulates affairs,
not seeking large salaries;
promoting the worthy and reaching the capable,
not expecting rewards;
the ruler obtains their aspirations,
the people rely on their virtue;
if it benefits the state,
they do not seek wealth and high position;
such is their promotion of the worthy and support for the capable.
The Rú purify their bodies and bathe in virtue,
presenting their opinions and then withdrawing,
speaking and correcting them,
even if the ruler does not know;
remaining silent and raising them up,
yet not treating it as urgent;
not using a shallow place to appear high,
not adding a little to appear much;
in times of order, they are not frivolous,
in times of chaos, they are not discouraged;
they do not associate with those who agree with them,
nor do they criticize those who disagree with them;
Qí tèlì dúxíng yǒu rúcǐ zhě. [Such] are those who stand alone and act independently.
Rú yǒu shàng bù chén tiānzǐ, [There are] Rú who above do not serve as subjects to the Son of Heaven,
xià bù shì zhūhóu; [and] below do not serve the various lords;
shèn jìng shàng kuān, [they] are careful and quiet, valuing tolerance,
dǐlì liányú; [and] cultivate integrity and principles;
qiángyì yǐ yǔ rén, [they] are resolute and firm in dealing with people,
bóxué yǐ zhī fú; [and] are broadly learned in order to understand [the meaning of] clothing;
jìn wénzhāng. [and] are close to literature.
Suī yǐ fēn guó, [Even if] offered a divided state,
shì rú zīzhū, [they] regard it as a trifling amount,
fú kěn chén shì; [and] would not be willing to serve as subjects and officials;
qí guī wèi yǒu rúcǐ zhě. [Such] are their standards.
Rú yǒu hézhì tóng fāng, [There are] Rú who have shared aspirations and common principles,
yíng dào tóng shù, [who] pursue the Way with the same methods,
bìng lì zé lè, [and] are happy when standing together,
xiāng xià bù yàn, [and] are never tired of yielding to each other,
jiǔ bié zé wén liúyán bù xìn; [and] when separated for a long time, do not believe rumors they hear;
yì tóng ér jìn, [they] advance when their righteousness is the same,
bù tóng ér tuì; [and] retreat when it is different;
qí jiāo yǒu rúcǐ zhě. [Such] are their relationships.
Fū wēnliáng zhě, [Now,] gentleness and kindness,
rén zhī běn yě; [are] the foundation of benevolence;
shèn jìng zhě, [carefulness and reverence,
rén zhī dì yě; [are] the grounding of benevolence;
kuānyù zhě, [generosity and tolerance,
rén zhī zuò yě; [are] the actions of benevolence;
xùn jiē zhě, [humility and accommodation,
rén zhī néng yě; [are] the capabilities of benevolence;
Ritual propriety is
the appearance of benevolence;
speech is
the expression of benevolence;
song and music are
the harmony of benevolence;
distribution is
the giving of benevolence.
Even if a Ru (scholar) possesses all of these,
still they dare not claim to be benevolent;
their respect and yielding are like this.
A Ru does not suffer hardship in poverty,
does not become arrogant in wealth and nobility,
does not cause trouble for the ruler,
does not burden superiors,
does not worry the officials,
therefore they are called Ru.
Nowadays, people's reputation as Ru is false,
they often use the term Ru to revile and hate each other."
After Duke Āi heard these words,
his words showed more trust,
his actions showed more respect,
and he said:
"Until the end of my life,
I dare not again use the term Ru as a jest."
Asking about Ritual, Chapter Six
Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"What is the Great Ritual like?
Your discussions of ritual,
how highly you regard it!"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"I, Qiū, am a humble person,
not worthy to understand the Great Ritual."
The Duke said:
"Please, sir, speak of it."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I have heard it said:
That the people are able to live is because ritual is paramount.
Without ritual, there is no way to regulate the service to the gods of Heaven and Earth;
without ritual, there is no way to distinguish the positions of ruler and subject, superior and inferior, elder and younger;
without ritual, there is no way to differentiate between male and female, father and son, brothers, marriage, relatives, and the degree of closeness in relationships.
Therefore, the gentleman uses this to show respect,
and then, using his abilities,
he teaches and guides the common people,
without abandoning their seasonal celebrations.
Once affairs are settled,
then he manages the carvings and decorations, the embroidered silks,
to distinguish the ranks of noble and base, superior and inferior.
After they are compliant,
then he speaks of the regulations for mourning and sacrifices,
and the order of the ancestral temple.
He grades the sacrificial animals,
sets up the winter sacrifices of pigs,
regulates the seasons,
With reverence, they offered sacrifices,
distinguished relatives by their closeness,
ordered them by their generations (zhāo and mù),
and then the clan would hold a feast.
They secured the people in their dwellings,
to strengthen kindness and righteousness,
lowered their palaces,
moderated their clothing and equipage,
their carriages were not carved with fine detail,
their vessels were not elaborately engraved,
their food was not of two tastes,
their hearts did not indulge in excessive desires,
in order to share the benefits with all the people.
The enlightened kings of antiquity
practiced ritual in this way."
The Duke said:
"Why is it that the gentlemen of today
do not practice this?"
Kǒngzǐ replied, saying:
"The gentlemen of today
love profit without limit,
indulge in excessive behavior without weariness,
are idle, negligent, and leisurely,
obstinately exhaust the people,
in order to fulfill their desires,
engendering resentment toward their government,
opposing the masses,
and attacking those who possess the Way;
Seeking what is desired but not according to the proper means;
inflicting cruel executions and punishments, but not for the sake of good governance.
nüè shā xíng zhū,
bù yǐ qí zhì.
Those who used the people in the past led them from the front;
those who use the people now lead them from behind.
This is why today's gentlemen are unable to practice the rites."
Yán Yǎn asked,
"Can I be allowed to hear your extreme expression of the rites?"
kě dé ér wén hū? 」
Kǒngzǐ said,
"I wanted to observe the ways of the Xià dynasty,
therefore I went to Qǐ,
but there was insufficient evidence.
I obtained the 《Xià Shí》 (the Xia Calendar) there.
I wanted to observe the ways of the Yīn dynasty,
therefore I went to Sòng,
but there was insufficient evidence.
I obtained the 《Qiánkūn》 there.
The meanings of 《Qiánkūn》,
the classifications of 《Xià Shí》,
I use these to observe them.
Now, the beginning of rites
starts with food and drink.
In the time of remote antiquity,
roasting millet and tearing apart pork,
To scoop up and drink from a dirty wine vessel,
to strike an earthenware drum with a clay beater,
even these can show respect to the spirits.
When a person dies,
they ascend to the roof and call out,
saying:
"High!
Mǒu fù (N.N., return)!"
Then they drink raw blood and eat fermented grain,
the physical body descends (into the earth),
the spirit ascends (to the sky),
this is what is meant by heaven observing and earth storing.
Therefore, the living face south,
and the dead face north,
all following their origins.
In the past, the ancient kings
had no palaces,
in winter they lived in dug-out caves,
in summer they lived in tree-branch nests;
they did not know how to use fire,
they ate the fruits of plants and the flesh of birds and beasts,
drank their blood,
and chewed their fur;
they had no silk or hemp,
and clothed themselves in feathers and skins.
Later, when sages arose,
they then developed the benefits of fire;
molding metal and combining earth,
They were used for platforms and pavilions, palaces and houses, doors and windows;
they were used to roast and burn,
to boil and grill,
to make sweet wine and fermented milk;
they processed its silk and hemp,
to make cloth and silk;
to nurture the living and bury the dead,
to serve ghosts and spirits.
Therefore, black wine was kept in the room,
sweet wine and thick wine were kept at the door,
sacrificial grains and sweet thick wine were in the hall,
clear wine was below,
arrange their sacrificial animals,
prepare their tripods and platters,
array their qín (琴), sè (瑟), guǎn (管), qìng (磬), zhōng (鐘), and gǔ (鼓),
with their prayers and blessings,
to bring down their highest spirits,
and their ancestors;
to correct the ruler and ministers,
to strengthen the father and son,
to harmonize the brothers,
to regulate those above and below,
husband and wife each have their place,
this is called receiving the blessing of Heaven.
Make their prayer titles,
use black wine for sacrifice,
offer its blood and hair,
make the platter savory;
Cook the cooked meat;
move the mat and sit;
cover with coarse cloth;
wear washed silk;
offer sweet wine and clear wine;
present the roasted offerings;
the lord and his lady present them in turn,
to please the spirits of the deceased;
this is called "uniting in the dusk."
Then retreat and combine the cooking,
cut up the dogs, pigs, cattle, and sheep,
fill the fǔ (round dishes), guǐ (square dishes), biān (bamboo trays), dòu (stemmed bowls), and xíng gēng (soup in vessels),
the invoker announces with filial piety,
the officiant announces with kindness,
this is called the great auspicious sacrifice.
This is the great completion of the rites."
"Explanation of the Five Rites," Section Seven.
Duke Āi asked Confucius, saying:
"I wish to evaluate the scholars of the state of Lǔ,
and employ them in government.
May I ask how should I select them?"
Confucius replied, saying:
"Born in this age,
aspiring to the ways of antiquity;
living in the customs of today,
wearing the clothes of antiquity.
"To abandon this and pursue what is incorrect,
wouldn't that be rare?"
He said:
"In that case, those wearing *zhāngfǔ* headwear and hemp shoes,
with sashes and belts, and holding ivory tablets,
are virtuous men."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"That is not necessarily so.
What I, Qiū, am talking about,
is not about this.
Those who wear formal clothes and dark skirts,
wear crowns and ride in carriages,
their minds are not on eating fragrant roasted meat;
those in mourning robes and straw sandals,
holding staffs and sipping gruel,
their minds are not on wine and meat.
Living in the present age,
aspiring to the ways of antiquity;
living in the present customs,
wearing the clothes of antiquity,
this is what I mean."
The Duke said:
"Excellent!
Is that all there is to it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"People have five categories:
there are common people,
there are scholars,
There are jūnzǐ (君子),
there are xiánrén (賢人),
there are shèngrén (聖人).
If one examines these five [types of men] carefully,
then the way to govern will be complete."
The Duke said:
"May I venture to ask, what kind of person can be called a yōngrén (庸人, mediocre person)?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
"Those who are called yōngrén (庸人)
do not keep in their hearts plans for a careful end,
do not utter words of instruction and correction,
do not choose worthy people to entrust themselves to,
and do not exert themselves to establish themselves;
they see the small and are blind to the great,
and do not know what to strive for;
they follow things like a stream,
not knowing what to hold onto firmly.
These are yōngrén (庸人)."
The Duke said:
"What is meant by shìrén (士人, scholar-official)?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said:
"Those who are called shìrén (士人)
have something settled in their hearts,
and have something to which their plans adhere.
Although they may not be able to exhaust the foundation of the Way and techniques,
they must have something they follow.
Although they may not be able to possess the beauty of a hundred virtues,
they must have a place where they reside [or something they abide by].
Therefore, in knowledge, they do not strive for much,
but they must carefully examine what they know.
In speech, they do not strive for much,
but they must carefully examine what they say.
In action, they do not strive for much,
but must carefully examine the path they take.
Once knowledge is known,
once words are spoken,
once actions are taken,
then it is like the form and body of life that cannot be changed;
wealth and honor are not enough to increase it,
poverty and lowliness are not enough to diminish it,
this is a shì rén (士人, scholar). "
The Duke said,
"What is called a Jūnzǐ (君子, gentleman)?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子, Confucius) said,
"What is called a Jūnzǐ (君子, gentleman) is one whose
words are always loyal and truthful,
and whose heart does not resent;
benevolence and righteousness reside in his person,
and his countenance shows no arrogance;
his thoughts and considerations are clear and bright,
and his words are not dogmatic;
he earnestly practices and believes in the Way,
and strengthens himself without ceasing,
appearing as if he will soon be surpassed,
but ultimately cannot be reached,
this is a Jūnzǐ (君子, gentleman)."
The Duke said:
"What is meant by a worthy person?"
Confucius said:
"What is meant by a worthy person is one whose
virtue does not exceed boundaries,
whose actions accord with the compass and square,
but must carefully examine the cause.
whose words are sufficient to be a model for the world,
yet do not harm himself;
whose way is sufficient to transform the common people,
yet does not harm the foundation;
if rich, then the world has no hoarded wealth;
if giving, then the world does not suffer from poverty;
this is a worthy person."
The Duke said:
"What is meant by a sage?"
Confucius said:
"What is meant by a sage is one whose
virtue is in accord with Heaven and Earth,
whose transformations are without limit,
who fully comprehends the beginning and end of all things,
who harmonizes with the naturalness of the myriad creatures,
who spreads his great Way,
and thereby completes their innate nature;
whose brightness rivals the sun and moon,
whose transformative influence acts like a spirit,
the common people do not know his virtue,
those who see him do not recognize his neighbor,
this is called a sage."
The Duke said:
"Excellent!
Were it not for your virtue,
then I would not have heard these words.
However,
I was born within the depths of the palace,
and grew up in the hands of women.
I have never known sorrow,
I have never known worry,
I have never known toil,
I have never known fear,
I have never known danger.
I fear I am insufficient to carry out the teachings of the Five Constant Virtues.
What should I do?"
Confucius replied:
"If it is as Your Lordship says,
that you already know this,
then I have nothing to tell you."
The Duke said:
"Without you,
I would have no way to open my heart.
Speak, I beg you."
Confucius said:
"When you enter the temple, go to the right.
Ascend from the eastern steps,
look up at the rafters,
and look down upon the sacrificial mats.
The ritual vessels are all present,
and not seeing the person,
if the ruler uses this to contemplate sorrow,
then sorrow can be understood;
in the dim light of dawn, rising early,
adjusting his robes and cap,
at daybreak attending court,
considering its dangers and difficulties,
a single thing lost to order,
is the beginning of chaos and ruin,
if the ruler uses this to contemplate worry,
then worry can be understood;
at sunrise hearing affairs of state,
until the middle of the night,
the descendants of the feudal lords,
coming and going as guests,
practicing ritual and yielding,
being careful of their dignified bearing,
if the ruler uses this to contemplate toil,
then toil can also be understood;
with lingering, extended thought,
going out from the four gates,
pacing and looking far off,
seeing the ruins of destroyed states;
there must certainly be a pattern to it,
if the ruler uses this to contemplate fear,
then fear can be understood;
now, the ruler is the boat;
the common people are the water.
Water can support a boat,
but it can also capsize it.
If the ruler considers danger in this way,
then danger can be understood.
Since the ruler already understands these five things,
and also pays attention to the matters of the Five Rites,
then what fault will there be in governance!"
Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"May I ask about the method of selecting people?"
Kǒngzǐ replied,
"Assign tasks according to office,
do not select the quick-witted,
do not select the flattering,
do not select the ingratiating.
Quick-wittedness is greed;
flattery is disorder;
ingratiation is falsehood.
Therefore, after a bow is tuned, then seek its strength;
after a horse is trained, then seek its quality;
a man must be sincere before seeking those with intelligence and ability.
To be insincere and yet have much ability
is like a jackal or wolf that cannot be approached."
Āi Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"I wish that my state, though small, could defend itself,
and if large, could attack.
What is the way to do this?"

Zǐlù (子路) said:
"Yóu (由, Zǐlù's personal name) once heard you say,
'Do not befriend those who are not as good as oneself,
and do not hesitate to correct your mistakes.'
You are hesitating now.
Let it be,
What should be done?"
Confucius said:
"When ordinary people have funerals,
they crawl to help them.
How much more so with old friends?
If he is not a friend,
I will not go."
When the outer coffin was ready,
Yuán Rǎng climbed on the wood
and said:
"It has been a long time,
since I have not vented through song."
So he sang:
"The mottled head of the wildcat,
holding the girl's hands so tenderly,
the master pretended not to hear and passed by."
Zǐ Lù said:
"Master, you are lowering your standards to the extreme here,
losing your dignity.
Shouldn't you stop?"
Confucius said:
"I have heard that
relatives should not lose their status as relatives,
and old friends should not lose their status as old friends."

Ritual is the foundation of governance.
Therefore, a gentleman cannot but cultivate himself;
thinking about cultivating himself,
he cannot but serve his parents;
thinking about serving his parents,
he cannot but understand people;
thinking about understanding people,
he cannot but understand Heaven.
There are five universal principles in the world,
and three ways to put them into practice.
They are:
ruler and subject,
father and son,
husband and wife,
elder and younger brothers,
and friends.
These five are the universal principles in the world.
Wisdom, benevolence, and courage, these three,
are the universal virtues in the world.
The way to put them into practice is one and the same.
Some are born knowing them,
some learn them through study,
some learn them through hardship,
and when they know them, it is all the same.
Some practice them easily,
some practice them for personal gain,
some practice them reluctantly,

The Duke said,
"Your words, Master,
are beautiful and profound!
I am truly inadequate
and not capable of achieving them."
Confucius (Kǒngzǐ) said:
"To love learning is close to wisdom,
to earnestly practice is close to benevolence,
to know shame is close to courage.
Knowing these three,
then one knows the way to cultivate oneself;
knowing the way to cultivate oneself,
then one knows the way to govern others;
knowing the way to govern others,
then one can achieve (order in) the world and the state."
The Duke said:
"Is government entirely contained in this?"
Confucius said:
"In all affairs of the world and the state, there are nine standards,
they are:
cultivating oneself,
honoring the worthy,
cherishing one's relatives,
respecting great ministers,
showing consideration for all officials,
valuing the common people,
attracting all kinds of craftsmen,
treating distant people kindly,
Cherishing the feudal lords.
If one cultivates oneself, then the Way will be established.
If one respects the worthy, then one will not be confused.
If one is kind to one's relatives, then one's uncles and brothers will not resent it.
If one respects great ministers, then one will not be bewildered.
If one is considerate of the multitude of ministers, then the gentlemen's reciprocation of courtesy will be valued.
If one values the common people, then the populace will be encouraged.
If one attracts the various artisans, then material resources will be sufficient.
If one treats distant people kindly, then people from all directions will return to him.
If one cherishes the feudal lords, then all under Heaven will fear him."
The Duke said:
"How can this be done?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Be purified and wear dignified clothes,
do not act unless it accords with ritual,
this is how to cultivate oneself;
discard slanderers and stay away from beautiful women,
despise profit and value virtue,
this is how to respect the worthy;
grant rank according to their ability,
increase their emoluments,
share their likes and dislikes,
this is how to strengthen kinship;
have ample officials for them to command and employ,
this is how to respect great ministers;
be loyal and trustworthy and value their emoluments,
this is how to encourage gentlemen;
employ them at the right time and collect taxes sparingly,
This is how to treat the common people as children;
daily inspection and monthly evaluation,
providing sustenance and stipends commensurate with duties,
this is how to attract all artisans;
seeing off those departing and welcoming those arriving,
praising the good and showing compassion for those who are not capable,
this is how to pacify distant people;
continuing broken lineages,
restoring fallen states,
governing chaos and maintaining the precarious,
holding court and receiving envoys at the proper times,
being generous in giving and receiving little in return,
this is how to cherish the feudal lords.
Governing the empire and the state has nine constant principles,
but the way to carry them out is one.
In all matters, preparedness leads to success,
lack of preparedness leads to failure;
if words are determined beforehand, there will be no stumbling;
if affairs are determined beforehand, there will be no distress;
if actions are determined beforehand, there will be no haste;
if the path is determined beforehand, there will be no exhaustion.
If one in a subordinate position does not gain the favor of his superior,
the people cannot be governed;
there is a way to gain the favor of one's superior,
if one is not trusted by friends,
one will not gain the favor of his superior;
there is a way to be trusted by friends,
if one is not obedient to parents,
not being trusted by friends.
To be obedient to one's parents has a method.
If reflecting upon oneself reveals a lack of sincerity,
one is not obedient to one's parents.
To be sincere in cultivating oneself has a method.
If one is not clear about goodness,
one is not sincere in cultivating oneself.
Sincerity is the Way of Heaven;
to strive for sincerity is the Way of Man.
Sincerity is such that, without forcing, one hits the mark;
without thinking, one obtains it;
in ease and composure, one hits the Way.
It is how the sage establishes his essence.
To strive for sincerity
is to choose goodness and firmly hold onto it."
Duke said:
"Your teachings, Master, are comprehensive for me.
May I ask where to begin in putting them into practice?"
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"Establish love beginning with one's parents,
and teach the people harmony.
Establish respect beginning with elders,
and teach the people obedience.
Teach them kindness and harmony,
and the people will value having family.
Teach them respect,
and the people will value following orders.
Once the people are filial to their parents
And if you comply and listen to commands,
and implement them throughout the land,
there is nothing that cannot be done."
The Duke said:
"Now that I have heard these words,
I fear that I will not be able to carry them out and incur blame."
Zǎi Wǒ asked Confucius, saying:

Confucius said:

Qi,

All living beings must die,

Combining ghosts and spirits to offer sacrifices to them,

Bones and flesh decay below,

Sages, based on the essence of things,
In establishing norms, he reached the extreme,

Therefore, he built palaces and houses,

The submission of the masses began from this,

He taught by means of two principles;

offering millet and sorghum,

This teaches the people to cultivate the roots, return to the beginnings, and value love,
superiors and inferiors using emotions,

The superior man returns to the origins and beginnings,
not forgetting from whence he came into being.
Therefore, he expresses his reverence,
releases his emotions,
exerts his strength in service,

This is called great teaching.

Yán Huí, Chapter Eighteen
Duke Dìng of Lǔ asked Yán Huí, saying:
"Have you also heard that Dōngyě Bì is good at charioteering?"
He replied:
"Good, he is good.
However,
his horses will surely run wild."
Duke Dìng's expression was displeased,
and he said to those around him:
"A gentleman certainly does accuse people falsely."
Yán Huí withdrew.
Three days later,
a herdsman came to report, saying:
"Dōngyě Bì's horses ran wild,
and the two outer horses dragged the two yoke horses into the stable."
The Duke heard of it,
rose from his mat in surprise,
and hastily ordered a carriage to summon Yán Huí.
When Huí arrived,
the Duke said:
"The other day I asked you about Dōngyě Bì's charioteering,
and you said:
'Good, he is good,
but his horses will run wild.'
"Not knowing my son, how do I know this?"
Yán Huí 顏回 replied,
"I know it through governance.
In the past,
Emperor Shùn 舜 was skilled in employing the people,
Zàofù 造父 was skilled in employing horses.
Shùn 舜 did not exhaust the strength of his people,
Zàofù 造父 did not exhaust the strength of his horses;
therefore, Shùn 舜 had no idle people,
Zàofù 造父 had no idle horses.
Now, the horsemanship of Dōngyě Bì 東野畢
raising the horse, holding the reins,
the posture of the bit is correct;
the steps, the gallops,
the morning ceremony is all complete;
traversing dangers, reaching far distances,
the horse's strength is exhausted;
yet he still seeks more from the horse without end.
I know this from this."
The Duke said,
"Good.
Truly it is as you say.
Your words,
their meaning is great.
I wish to advance a little more."
Yán Huí 顏回 replied,
"I have heard that
a bird, when exhausted, will peck,
When a beast is cornered, it bites;
when a person is cornered, they deceive;
when a horse is cornered, it runs wild.
From ancient times until now,
there has never been a case of exhausting one's subordinates and yet remaining free from danger."
The Duke was pleased.
Thereupon, he told Confucius this.
Confucius replied,
"That which makes Yán Huí who he is,
is this kind of thing.
How much more is required?"
Confucius was in Wèi.
At the break of dawn, early in the morning,
Yán Huí was attending at his side.
He heard the sound of someone weeping, and it was very sad.
Confucius said,
"Huí!
Do you know why this person is crying?"
He replied,
"Huí thinks that this weeping is not only for the dead,
but also for those who are being separated in life."
Confucius said,
"How do you know this?"
He replied,
"Huí heard that the birds of Mount Huán,
bore four offspring.
Once their wings are formed,
they will be scattered across the four seas,
their mother cries sadly as she sees them off.
The sound of grief is similar to this,
indicating they will go and not return.
I, Huí, secretly knew it through the category of sounds."
Kǒngzǐ sent someone to ask the crying person,
who indeed said:
"My father died and my family is poor,
so I am selling my son to pay for his burial,
a final farewell to him."
The Master said:
"Huí,
is truly good at recognizing sounds!"
Yánhuí asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"What is the conduct of a complete person like?"
The Master said:
"To be versed in the principles of feelings and nature,
to be knowledgeable in the changes of things,
to understand the reasons for the visible and invisible,
to observe the origin of the wandering Qi;
such a person can be called complete.
Having become a complete person,
and then adding benevolence, righteousness, rites, and music,
that is the conduct of a complete person;
as for thoroughly investigating the spirit and knowing the rites,
It is the flourishing of virtue."
Yán Huí asked Confucius, saying:
"Zāng Wénzhòng and Wǔzhòng, who is the more virtuous?"
Confucius said:
"Wǔzhòng is the more virtuous!"
Yán Huí said:
"Wǔzhòng is regarded by the world as a sage,
yet he could not avoid being guilty of offenses.
Thus, his wisdom is not worthy of praise.
He loved to talk about military campaigns
but suffered defeat at Zhū.
Thus, his wisdom is not worthy of the name.
Now, Wénzhòng, though his person is dead,
his words do not decay.
How can he not be considered virtuous?"
Confucius said:
"His person is dead, but his words endure,
that is what makes Wénzhòng what he is.
However, he still has three instances of unkindness,
and three instances of imprudence;
therefore he is not as good as Wǔzhòng."
Huí said:
"May I be told about them?"
Confucius said:
"He demoted Zhǎn Qín,
established six barriers,
I weave cattails,
three times without benevolence.
Setting up empty vessels,
indulging rebellious sacrifices,
worshiping sea birds,
three times without wisdom.
When Wǔ Zhòng was in Qí,
Qí was about to have calamity,
he did not accept their land,
in order to avoid their trouble,
this is the difficulty of wisdom.
Now, Zāng Wǔzhòng's wisdom,
but was not accepted in Lǔ,
there is indeed a reason for it,
acting without compliance,
bestowing without generosity.
The "Xia Documents" say:
'Be mindful of this, be mindful of this,
be compliant in affairs, be generous in bestowing.' "
Yán Huí asked about the junzi.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Love approaches benevolence,
measuring approaches wisdom,
acting for oneself without being weighty,
acting for others without being frivolous,
that is a junzi!"
Huí said:
"Dare I ask about the next level?"
The Master said:
"To act without learning,
to attain without thinking.
My little ones, strive for this!"
18.6 Zhòngsūn Héjì asked Yán Huí, saying:
"The words of a rén person are sure to benefit rén and zhì.
Can I hear about this?"
Huí said:
"If one word is to benefit zhì,
nothing is better than forethought (yù);
if one word is to benefit rén,
nothing is better than forbearance (shù).
If one knows what cannot be followed,
then one knows what should be followed."
18.7 Yán Huí asked about xiǎorén.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"To denigrate the good in others to show off one's own eloquence,
to be cunning and accusatory, harboring deceit in order to appear wise,
to rejoice in the mistakes of others,
to be ashamed to learn and embarrassed by one's own inability –
these are characteristics of xiǎorén."
18.8 Yán Huí asked Zǐlù, saying:
"Those whose strength surpasses their virtue
and thereby meet their death,
are few indeed.
Why not be careful about this?"
Kǒngzǐ said to Yán Huí:
Yán Huí asked Zǐ Lù, saying:
"People all know the beauty of this principle,
yet no one controls themselves with it,
and no one acts upon it, what is the reason?
For those who hear it, why not say they think about it?"
18.9 Yán Huí asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"The words of inferior people,
sometimes resemble those of superior people,
and cannot but be examined."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Superior people speak with actions,
inferior people speak with their tongues.
Therefore, superior people, when pursuing righteousness,
dislike each other,
but retreat and love each other;
inferior people, when pursuing disorder,
love each other,
but retreat and hate each other."
18.10 Yán Huí asked how one should associate with friends.
Confucius said:
"When a gentleman deals with friends,
he must recognize their faults, but cannot bring himself to say, 'I do not know that they are benevolent people.'
He does not forget long-standing kindnesses,
nor does he dwell on old grudges.
That is benevolence indeed!"
18.11 Shū Sūn Wǔ Shū visited Yán Huí, who was not yet employed in office.
Huí said:
"Treat him as a guest."
Wǔ Shū often praised the faults of others and commented on them.
Yán Huí said:
"So, sir, your coming is to humiliate me.

I have heard Confucius say:
'Speaking of the evil of others

speaking of the crookedness of others

Therefore, a gentleman attacks his own evil,

19.1 Zǐlù's First Meeting, Chapter Nineteen
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What do you enjoy?"
He replied:
"I enjoy long swords."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"That is not what I am asking about.
I am merely saying that with your abilities,
and adding learning to them,
how could you not succeed?"
Zǐlù said:
"Does learning really add anything?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If a ruler has no ministers to remonstrate with him, he will lose his correctness;
if a scholar has no friends to teach him, he will lose his hearing.
When controlling a wild horse, one does not release the whip;
when handling a bow, one does not remove the frame.
Wood becomes straight when subjected to the plumb line,
a person becomes wise when accepting admonishment.
Accepting learning and valuing questions,
who would not be compliant?
To slander the benevolent and hate scholars
will surely lead to punishment.
A gentleman must learn."
Zǐlù said:
"There is bamboo on Nánshān (South Mountain),
which is straight without being bent,
Zǐlù met Kǒngzǐ.
and when cut and used,
it penetrates rhinoceros hide.
In light of this,
what need is there for learning?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If feathers are attached to the end and it is fitted with a nock,
and its arrowhead is sharpened,
would it not penetrate even deeper?"
Zǐlù bowed twice and said:
"I respectfully receive your teaching."
Zǐlù was about to leave,
and took leave of Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shall I gift you with a carriage?
Or shall I gift you with words?"
Zǐlù said:
"Please, with words."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Without striving, there is no success;
without labor, there is no merit;
Disloyalty leads to no relatives,
untrustworthiness leads to no return,
disrespect leads to loss of propriety.
Be cautious of these five only."
Zǐ Lù said:
"Yóu requests to uphold them for life.
May I ask, how to treat relatives among friends?
How to make few words actionable?
How to be a virtuous person for long without transgressions?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"What you ask is contained within these five.
To treat relatives among friends
is loyalty;
to make few words actionable
is trustworthiness;
to be a virtuous person for long without transgressing is propriety."
Kǒngzǐ, as the Minister of Justice for Lǔ,
met with Jì Kāngzǐ.
Kāngzǐ was displeased,
and Kǒngzǐ met with him again.
Zǎi Yǔ came forward and said:
"In the past, Yǔ has often heard you, Master, say:
'If rulers do not employ me,
then I will not act.'
Now, Master, in the position of Minister of Justice,
your daily time is lessened, and you frequently lower yourself.
"Can it not be stopped?"
Confucius said:
"It can.
In the State of Lǔ, the many bully the few,
and they have long used weapons to do violence to each other.
If the officials do not govern,
then there will be chaos.
Of those who would hire me,
who is greater than this!"
The people of Lǔ heard this and
said:
"The sage is about to govern,
why not first keep himself far from punishments?"
From then on,
there were no more disputes in the state.
Confucius said to Zǎi Yǔ:
"Even ten *lǐ* away from the mountain,
the sound of the cicada
is still in your ear.
Therefore, in government, nothing is as good as being responsive."
Confucius's nephew, Kǒng Miè,
and Mì Zǐjiàn both took office.
Confucius went to visit Kǒng Miè and asked him,
"Since you took office,
what have you gained and what have you lost?"
He replied:
"I have gained nothing,
and what I have lost is threefold.
Royal affairs are like dragons,
how can I find time to study and practice,
thus my studies cannot be clarified;
my salary is meager,
even thin porridge cannot reach my relatives,
thus my flesh and blood become increasingly estranged;
public affairs are many and urgent,
I cannot attend funerals or inquire after the sick,
thus the way of friendship is neglected.
What I have lost is threefold,
that is what I mean."
Kǒngzǐ was displeased.
He went to visit Zǐjiàn,
and asked about it as he had asked Kǒng Miè.
Zǐjiàn replied:
"Since I have come to serve,
what I have lost is nothing, but what I have gained is threefold.
What I began by reciting,
now I am able to put into practice,
thus my studies are increasingly clarified;
what my salary provides for,
extends to my relatives,
thus my flesh and blood become increasingly close;
even though there are public affairs,
I still manage to attend funerals and inquire after the sick,
thus my friendships become increasingly sincere."
Confucius sighed and said to Zǐjiàn:
"What a gentleman that man is!
If Lǔ did not have gentlemen,
where would Zǐjiàn have acquired this?"
19.5 Confucius was sitting in attendance on Duke Āi.
He was given peaches and millet.
Duke Āi said:
"Please."
Confucius first ate the millet and then ate the peach.
Those on either side of the Duke covered their mouths and laughed.
The Duke said:
"The millet is for cleansing the palate after the peach,
not to be eaten."
Confucius replied:
"Qiū knows this.
However, millet is the chief of the five grains,
and in suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, it is regarded as the supreme offering.
Among fruits there are six categories,
but the peach is the lowest,
not used in sacrifices,
nor offered in suburban temples.
I have heard that
a gentleman uses the base to set off the noble,
but I have never heard of using the noble to set off the base.
Now, using the chief of the five grains
to set off the lowest of fruits
This is like snow falling from above.
Your servant believes it hinders instruction,
and harms righteousness,
therefore I dare not do it."
The Duke said,
"Excellent!"
19.6 Zǐgòng said:
Zǐ Gòng said:
"Duke Líng of Chén openly indulged in licentiousness at court.
Xiè Yě remonstrated directly and was killed.
Is this the same as Bǐgān's remonstrating and dying,
can he be called benevolent?"
The Master said:
"Bǐgān, in relation to Zhòu,
was a close relative, his uncle;
in office, he was the Junior Tutor.
His loyal and devoted heart
was entirely focused on the ancestral temple.
He was determined to argue with him to the death,
hoping that after his death,
Zhòu would regret and awaken.
His fundamental intention and emotion were those of a benevolent man.
Xiè Yě, in relation to Duke Líng,
held the position of a Grand Master,
had no blood relation to him,
cherished favor and did not leave,
serving in a chaotic court.
With his insignificant self,
yù zhèng yī guó zhī yínhūn,
sǐ ér wúyì,
kěwèi juàn yǐ.
"Shī" yuē:
"Mín zhī duō pì,
wú zì lì pì."
Qí Xiè Yě zhī wèi hū? 」

Using one's insignificant self, to correct the licentiousness and darkness of a whole country, to die without benefit, this can be called obstinate. The *Book of Poetry* says: "The people have many perverse ways, do not establish perversity yourself." Is it speaking of Xiè Yě? 19.7
Kǒngzǐ xiàng Lǔ.
Qí rén huàn qí jiāng bà,
yù bài qí zhèng.
Nǎi xuǎn hǎo nǚzǐ bāshí rén,
yī yǐ wénshì ér wǔ róng jī,

yǐ yí Lǔ jūn.
Chén nǚyuè, liè wén mǎ yú Lǔ chéng nángāo mén wài,
Jì Huánzǐ wēifú wǎng guān zhī,
zàisān,
jiāng shòu yān.
Gào Lǔ jūn wèi Zhōu dào yóuguān,
guān zhī zhōng rì,

Zǐlù yán yú Kǒngzǐ yuē:

Kǒngzǐ yuē:

"If he sends the sacrificial meat to the Grand Masters,

Huan Zi having received the female musicians,
the ruler and his ministers indulged in licentiousness and dissipation,
