Confucius then departed,
lodging at Guo Tun.
The musicians had already been sent off,
and said:
"Is the Master not guilty?"
Confucius said:
"May I sing a song?"
The song said:
"That woman's mouth,
can cause one to flee;
that woman's solicitations,
can lead to death and ruin.
Relax, relax,
let's just pass the year."
Dàntái Zǐyǔ had the appearance of a gentleman,
but his conduct did not live up to his appearance;
Zǎi Wǒ had refined and elegant words,
but his wisdom did not match his eloquence.
Confucius said:
"A village saying goes:
'Judge a horse by its cart-pulling ability,
judge a scholar by his dwelling,'
it cannot be abandoned."
If one judges people by appearance,
then one will err with Zǐyǔ;
if you judge a person by their words,
you will fail to recognize Zǎi Yǔ.
19.9 Confucius said:
"The junzi uses what he cannot do to awe others;
the xiǎorén uses what he cannot to not trust others.
Therefore, the junzi develops people's talents,
while the xiǎorén suppresses people to gain victory."
19.10 Kǒng Miè asked about the way to conduct oneself.
Confucius said:
"To know and not act is worse than not knowing;
to be close and not trust is worse than not being close.
When joy is about to arrive,
enjoy it but do not be arrogant;
when trouble is about to arrive,
consider it but do not worry."
Kǒng Miè said:
"Is this how to conduct oneself?"
The Master said:
"Attack where they are incapable,
supplement what they lack.
Do not doubt others because of your own incapacities,
and do not be arrogant because of your own abilities.
Speaking all day long,
leave no worries for oneself;
acting all day long,
leave no troubles for oneself.
Only the wise possess this."
In distress, section twenty.
King Zhāo of Chǔ hired Confucius,
and Confucius went to pay his respects.
The route took him through Chén and Cài.
The high officials of Chén and Cài consulted with each other, saying:
"Confucius is a sage,
and his criticisms and sarcasms
all hit upon the flaws of the feudal lords.
If he is employed by Chǔ,
then Chén and Cài will be in danger."
Thereupon, they sent soldiers to block Confucius.
Confucius was unable to proceed,
running out of provisions for seven days.
He had no communication with the outside world,
coarse porridge was insufficient,
and his followers all fell ill.
Kǒngzǐ became even more impassioned in his lectures and recitations,
and the playing of stringed instruments and singing did not diminish.
He then summoned Zǐlù and asked him,
saying:
"The *Shī* (Book of Poetry) says:
'Not a rhinoceros, not a tiger,
it roams that wide wilderness.'
Is my way wrong?
Why have I come to this?"
Zǐlù was displeased,
changed his expression, and replied,
"A gentleman should not be in dire straits.
Could it be that the Master is not yet benevolent?
That people do not trust us;
could it be that the Master is not yet wise?
That people do not follow us.
Moreover, Yóu,
in the past, heard from the Master:
'Those who do good,
Heaven repays them with blessings;
those who do evil,
Heaven repays them with misfortune.'
Now, the Master has accumulated virtue and cherished righteousness,
and has practiced them for a long time,
why is he in such poverty?"
Confucius said:
"Yóu, you do not understand!
Let me tell you.
If you think the benevolent are necessarily trustworthy,
then Bó Yí and Shū Qí would not have starved to death on Mount Shǒu Yáng;
if you think the wise are necessarily employed,
then Prince Bǐ Gān would not have had his heart cut out;
if you think the loyal are necessarily rewarded,
then Guān Lóngpáng would not have been executed;
if you think those who offer advice are necessarily listened to,
then Wǔ Zǐxū would not have been killed.
As for encountering fortune or misfortune,
it is a matter of timing;
as for being worthy or unworthy,
it is a matter of talent.
Gentlemen who are broadly learned and deeply thoughtful,
yet do not encounter the right time,
are numerous.
Why single out Qiū?
Moreover, the zhī and lán orchids grow in deep forests,
and do not cease to be fragrant because there are no people present;
the gentleman cultivates the Way and establishes virtue,
and does not ruin his integrity because of poverty and hardship,
to act is up to man,
life and death are up to fate.
Therefore, the hegemonic ambitions of Jìn Chóng'ěr
arose in Cáo and Wèi;
the hegemonic ambitions of King Gōujiàn of Yuè
arose in Kuàijī.
Therefore, those who dwell in low positions without worry,
their thoughts do not reach far;
"Those who live comfortably and constantly seek ease,
their aspirations will not be broad.
How can they know the beginning and the end?"
Zǐlù left.
He summoned Zǐgòng,
and told him what he had told Zǐlù.
Zǐgòng said:
"The Master's way is exceedingly great,
therefore the world cannot accommodate the Master.
Why doesn't the Master diminish it somewhat?"
The Master said:
"Cì!
A good farmer can plant,
but cannot necessarily harvest;
a good craftsman can be skillful,
but cannot make things favorable;
a gentleman can cultivate his way,
establish its guidelines and order,
but he cannot necessarily be accommodated.
Now, not cultivating his way,
but seeking to be accommodated,
Cì,
your aspirations are not broad!
Your thoughts are not far-reaching!"
Zǐgòng left.
Yánhuí entered,
and asked the same question.
Yánhuí said:
"The Master's (Fūzǐ's) way is supremely great,
the world is unable to contain it.
Although that is so,
if the Master were to promote and implement it,
and the world did not employ us,
it would be the shame of those who possess the state.
What illness does the Master have from this!
It is only when one is not accommodated that the true gentleman is revealed."
Kǒngzǐ happily sighed and said,
"Is that so,
Yán shì zhī zǐ (son of the Yán family)!
I also wish to make you wealthy,
I would become your steward."
Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Does the gentleman also have worries?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"No.
The gentleman's self-cultivation is such that,
before he obtains it,
he delights in the intention;
having obtained it,
he also delights in its governance.
Therefore, he has joy throughout his life,
without a single day of worry.
The petty man is not like this;
before he obtains it,
One worries about not obtaining it;
having obtained it,
one then fears losing it.
Therefore, one has worry for a lifetime,
without a single day of joy."
The ruler of Lǔ heard of this and sent him a town.
Zēngzǐ firmly declined and did not accept it.
Someone said:
"It was not you who sought it,
the ruler himself presented it,
why decline so firmly?"
Zēngzǐ said:
"I have heard that those who receive from others are always in awe of them,
and those who give to others are always arrogant.
Even if the ruler bestows a gift,
he will not be arrogant towards me.
How could I not be in awe?"
In the end, he did not accept it.
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and
said:
"Shēn's words are sufficient to preserve his integrity."
his followers went without food for seven days.
Zǐ Gòng, using the goods he carried,
secretly broke through the siege and went out.
He announced the rice purchase to the country people,
and obtained one *shí* of rice.
Yán Huí and Zhòng Yóu cooked it under a dilapidated house.
Some dust and soot fell into the rice.
Zēngzǐ wore tattered clothes and plowed in Lǔ.
Kǒngzǐ was in distress in Chén and Cài;
Yán Huí took it and ate it.
Zǐ Gòng saw it from the well,
He was displeased
He thought that he was stealing food.
He went in and asked Confucius, saying:
"If a benevolent and upright scholar is in poverty,
does he change his principles?"
Confucius said:
"If he changes his principles, how can he be called benevolent and upright?"
Zǐ Gòng said:
"As for Huí,
would he not change his principles?"
Confucius said:
"Indeed."
Zǐ Gòng told Confucius about the rice.
Confucius said:
"I have long believed in the benevolence of Huí.
Even if you say so,
I would not doubt him.
Perhaps there must be a reason?
You stop,
I will ask him."
Confucius summoned Yán Huí and said:
"Last night, I dreamed of our ancestors;
could it be that they are offering me guidance and blessing?
Cook rice and bring it to me,
I shall offer it to them."
He replied:
"A moment ago, some dust fell into the rice.
If I were to set it aside,
it would be unclean;
if I were to throw it away,
it would be a pity.
So I, Huí, ate it,
and it is not fit for offering."
Confucius said:
"Is that so!
I, too, ate some of it."
Yán Huí left.
Confucius turned and said to his other disciples:
"My trust in Huí
is not something that began today."
Thereupon, the other disciples were convinced by this.
Chapter 21: Entering Official Service
Zǐ Zhāng asked Confucius about entering official service.
Confucius said:
"Securing peace of mind and gaining a good reputation is difficult."
Zǐ Zhāng said:
"How does one do it?"
Confucius said:
"Do not monopolize the good you possess,
do not be negligent in teaching what you are capable of,
do not disclose past faults,
do not regret careless words,
do not persist in wrongdoing,
do not delay in taking action.
When a gentleman enters office,
if he adheres to these six principles,
then he will be secure in person, reputation will arrive, and his governance will be followed.
Furthermore, anger and reprimands
are the source from which official disputes and prisons arise;
rejecting advice
is why considerations are blocked;
being casual and disrespectful
is why ritual propriety is lost;
being lazy and indolent
is why time is wasted;
extravagance
is why wealth is insufficient;
and being selfish and autocratic
is why affairs are unsuccessful.
When a gentleman enters office,
if he eliminates these six things,
then he will be secure in person, reputation will arrive, and his governance will be followed.
Therefore, the gentleman faces south in the midst of his great official domain and governs it impartially,
meticulously plans and then concisely executes,
values loyalty and trustworthiness,
To examine is the great principle,
to preserve is good and to eliminate is evil,
to advance is beneficial and to remove is harmful,
without seeking any reward for it,
and the people's feelings can be obtained.
Now, in governing, do not resist the people's dislikes,
in being victorious, do not violate the people's words,
in assessing, do not dispute the people's arguments,
in nurturing, do not disturb their seasons,
in loving, do not be lenient with laws and punishments.
If this is so,
then personal safety and reputation will arrive, and the people will benefit.
When a gentleman governs,
what he sees is near,
therefore his clarity cannot be obscured;
what he seeks is near,
therefore he obtains it without labor;
the means by which he governs are simple,
therefore he does not need many and his reputation is established;
all models of law reside within,
therefore the law is not far and its source does not dry up.
Therefore, the empire accumulates and its foundation is not weak,
the short and the long are measured correctly,
people's wills are governed and do not disrupt the government,
virtue permeates the heart,
is stored in the will,
is manifested in appearance,
and is expressed in voice.
If this is so,
then one's person will be secure and renown will arrive,
and the people will all govern themselves.
Therefore, if one who holds office does not govern well, there will be disorder.
If disorder arises, then those who contend for power will arrive.
When contention arrives,
it will revert to disorder.
An enlightened ruler must be broad-minded and forgiving in accommodating his people,
treat them with kindness and gentleness,
and the people will naturally be content.
Action is the beginning of governance;
persuasion is the guidance of emotions.
If good governance is easily implemented,
then the people will not resent it.
If speech is harmonious and persuasive,
then the people will not change their minds.
If the law is embodied in oneself,
then the people will imitate it.
If clarity resides in oneself,
then the people will make it manifest.
If one provides for oneself without restraint,
then the generation of wealth and profit will be meager.
If one is greedy and does not attain satisfaction,
then good governance will surely be neglected.
If one is careless in governing,
then good advice will surely not be heeded.
If one carefully accepts advice,
then remonstrances will arrive daily,
Fán yǐ bù tīng yǐ. It is vexing when (one) is not listened to.
Yán zhī shàn zhě, Good words,
zài suǒ rì wén; are heard daily;
xíng zhī shàn zhě, Good actions,
zài suǒ néng wéi. are what one is capable of doing.
Gù jūnzǐ shàng zhě, mín zhī yí yě; Therefore, the ruler is the model for the people;
yǒu sī zhí zhèng zhě, The officials who hold power,
mín zhī biǎo yě; are the standard for the people;
ěr chén biàn pì zhě, Close, flattering ministers,
qún pú zhī lún yě. are the type of the common servants.
Gù yí bù zhèng, Therefore, if the model is not upright,
zé mín shī; the people will go astray;
biǎo bù duān, If the standard is not correct,
zé bǎixìng luàn; the common people will be in chaos;
ěr chén biàn pì bù zhèng lián, If the close, flattering ministers are not upright and honest,
zé qún chén wū yǐ. the assembled ministers will be corrupted.
Shì yǐ rén zhǔ bùkě bù jìng hū sān lún. Therefore, a ruler cannot but respect these three types of people.
Jūnzǐ xiūshēn fǎn dào, The gentleman cultivates himself and returns to the proper way,
chá lǐ yán ér fú zhī, observes words of principle and follows them,
zé shēn ān yù zhì, then his person will be secure, and praise will come,
zhōng shǐ zài yān. and (he) will have a good end and beginning.
Gù fū nǚzǐ bì zì zé sī má, Therefore, a woman must select her own silk and hemp,
liáng gōng bì zì zé wán cái, a good craftsman must select his own perfect material,
xián jūn bì zì zé zuǒyòu. a wise ruler must select his own attendants.
Láo yú qǔ rén, Laboring in selecting men,
yì yú zhì shì, leads to ease in managing affairs,
jūnzǐ yù yù, The gentleman who desires praise,
zé bì jǐn qí zuǒyòu. must be careful in selecting his attendants.
For those who are in positions of authority, it is like climbing a tree;
striving for height while fearing to descend is most serious.
The separation and scattering of six horses
will surely occur at the crossroads where four roads meet;
the rebellion of the myriad people against the proper way
will surely occur because of the ruler's loss of proper governance.
Those above are honored and dignified, yet in danger;
the people are humble and lowly, yet possess divine power.
Cherish them, and they will survive;
despise them, and they will perish.
Those who govern the people must understand this essential point.
Therefore, those who face south in office
are noble but not arrogant,
wealthy but able to provide for others,
have a foundation and can plan for the future,
manage affairs and can establish a legacy,
reside in a place for a long time without stagnating,
are close in affection yet comprehend the distant,
observe one thing and comprehend many,
govern one thing and are not thrown into disorder by the myriad things;
this is because they cultivate themselves as the foundation.
When a Junzi (gentleman) governs the people,
he cannot be ignorant of the people's nature and understand their feelings.
Having understood their nature,
and also become familiar with their feelings,
then the people will follow his commands.
Therefore, when the world is governed justly, the people will be close to him;
when governance is equitable, the people will have no complaints.
Therefore, when a Jūnzǐ governs the people,
he does not look down on them from a high position,
he does not guide them toward the distant,
he does not demand of the people what they cannot do,
he does not force the people to do what they are unable to do.
With the accomplishments of an enlightened king,
One must certainly seek their good [qualities]
in order to pardon their faults.
If the people have committed great crimes,
one must certainly investigate their reasons
in order to assist transformation with benevolence.
If there are crimes deserving death,
to cause them to live
is good.
Therefore, those above and below are close and do not separate;
the Way's transformation flows and does not stagnate.
Therefore, virtue is the beginning of governance.
If governance is not harmonious,
then the people will not follow its teachings;
if they do not follow the teachings,
then the people will not become accustomed [to them];
if they are not accustomed,
then they cannot be obtained and employed.
If a *jūnzǐ* 君子 desires that his words be believed,
nothing is better than first emptying his interior;
if he desires that his policies be quickly implemented,
nothing is better than taking the lead himself;
if he desires that the people quickly submit,
nothing is better than governing them with the Way.
Therefore, although they submit, they will necessarily be forced;
if it does not come from loyalty and trustworthiness,
then there is no way to gain the affection of the common people;
if the internal and external do not correspond,
then there is no way to gain the trust of the masses.
This is the ultimate way to govern the people,
and the grand principle for entering into officialdom."
Zǐ Zhāng 子張, having heard Kǒngzǐ's 孔子 words,
then withdrew and recorded them.
Chapter Twenty-Two: Weariness and Vows
Zǐ Gòng 子貢 asked Kǒngzǐ 孔子, saying:
"Sì 賜 is weary of learning,
and exhausted by the Dao.
I wish to rest in serving a ruler,
is that permissible?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"The *Book of Poetry* says:
'Be gentle and respectful, morning and night,
Attending to your duties with diligence.'
Serving a ruler is difficult.
How can you rest?"
He said:
"In that case, I wish to rest in serving my parents."
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"The *Book of Poetry* says:
'A filial son is never deficient,
May you forever bless your kind.'
Serving one's parents is difficult.
How can you rest?"
He said:
"In that case, I beg to rest with my wife and children."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Poetry* says:
'He models himself on his wife,
extending to his brothers,
thereby governing his family and state.'
Dealing with one's wife is difficult.
Where can one find rest?"
He said:
"Then Cì wishes to rest among friends."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Poetry* says:
'Friends should be controlled,
controlled with dignity and ceremony.'
Dealing with friends is difficult.
Where can one find rest?"
He said:
"Then Cì will wish to rest in farming."
Confucius said:
"The *Book of Poetry* says:
'In the daytime you work with thatch,
at night you twist ropes,
quickly you ascend the roof,
then begin to sow the various grains.'
Farming is difficult.
Where can one find rest?"
He said:
"Then will Cì have nowhere to rest?"
Confucius said:
"It exists.
When one looks at its expanse,
it appears vast and marshy;
when one views its height,
it seems towering;
when one examines its surroundings,
it appears isolated.
This is the reason for its existence."
Zǐ Gòng said:
"How great is death!
The junzi rests in it!
The petty person finds respite in it!
How great is death!"
Kǒngzǐ was traveling from Wèi to enter Jìn.
Upon reaching the river,
he heard that Zhào Jiǎnzi had killed Dòu Chōu, Míng Dú, and Shùn Huá.
He then stood by the river and sighed, saying:
"How beautiful is the water,
so vast and flowing!
That I will not cross it,
is fate, indeed!"
Zǐ Gòng hurried forward and asked:
"May I venture to ask what you mean?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Dòu Chōu, Míng Dú, and Shùn Huá were
virtuous senior officials of Jìn.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ 趙簡子, when he had not yet achieved his ambition,
needed these two people before he could engage in politics.
But when he had already achieved his ambition,
he killed them.
Qiū 丘 (Confucius) heard of this and said:
"If one cuts open wombs and kills the young,
then qílín 麒麟 (Chinese unicorns) will not come to its borders;
if one drains the pond to catch the fish,
then jiāolóng 蛟龍 (aquatic dragons) will not dwell in its depths;
if one overturns nests and breaks eggs,
then fènghuáng 鳳凰 (Chinese phoenixes) will not soar over its city.
Why is this?
It is because the junzi 君子 (gentleman) avoids harming its own kind.
Even birds and beasts know to avoid
what is unrighteous,
how much more so should humans!"
Thereupon he turned back
and rested in Zōu 鄒,
composing "Pán Qín 槃琴" (The Leaning Lute) to mourn them.
Zǐlù 子路 asked Kǒngzǐ 孔子, saying:
"If there is a person here
who rises early and sleeps late,
cultivating and planting trees,
with hands and feet calloused,
in order to support his parents,
yet his name is not called filial,
Why is that?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Could it be that you are not respectful in your person?
Or that your words are not agreeable?
Or that your countenance is not pleasing?
The people of old had a saying:
'If people are in harmony with you, they will not deceive you.'
Now, you exert all your strength to nourish your parents,
and you have none of these three shortcomings,
why do you say you lack the reputation of being filial?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Yóu!
Remember this,
I will tell you.
Even if one possesses the strength of a national champion,
and cannot lift himself,
it is not because his strength is lacking,
but because the situation makes it impossible.
If one's inner conduct is not cultivated,
it is one's own fault;
if one's conduct is cultivated but one's reputation is not known,
it is the fault of one's friends;
if one's conduct is cultivated, then one's reputation will naturally be established.
Therefore, a gentleman, when at home, sincerely cultivates his conduct,
and when abroad, associates with worthy people,
why then would he lack the reputation of being filial?"
Kǒngzǐ encountered hardship between Chén and Cài;
they were without provisions for seven days,
and the disciples were hungry and ill.
Kǒngzǐ played and sang.
Zǐlù entered and said,
"Master's singing,
is it proper?"
Kǒngzǐ did not answer.
After the song ended, he said,
"Yóu, come!
Let me tell you.
A gentleman's fondness for music
is to prevent arrogance;
a petty person's fondness for music
is to prevent being frightened.
Who knows this?
Are you not the one who does not understand me yet follows me?"
Zǐlù was pleased,
took up an axe and danced,
and finished three times before exiting.
The next day,
they were freed from the hardship.
Zǐgòng held the reins
and said,
"You disciples, following the Master and encountering this difficulty,
will certainly not forget it!"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"What is good or bad?
Being between Chén and Cài,
is fortunate for Qiū.
Those two or three disciples who follow Qiū,
are all fortunate.
I have heard it said,
a ruler who is not troubled cannot become king,
a resolute person who is not troubled cannot make his conduct manifest.
How do we know it is not the beginning of being spurred on by indignation and strengthening one's resolve that lies in this?"
When Kǒngzǐ went to Sòng,
the people of Kuāng, led by Jiǎnzǐ, surrounded him with armored soldiers.
Zǐlù was angry,
brandished his halberd and was about to fight.
Kǒngzǐ stopped him,
saying:
"How can there be someone who cultivates benevolence and righteousness and yet escapes the common ways of the world?
It is my fault that the *Book of Odes* and the *Book of Documents* are not taught,
and that rites and music are not practiced;
but if I am blamed for transmitting the ways of the former kings and loving the ancient laws,
then that is not my fault.
Fate!
Sing!
I will harmonize with you."
Zǐlù played the zither and sang,
Kǒngzǐ harmonized with him,
after the melody ended three times,
the people of Kuāng took off their armor and dispersed.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If you do not observe high cliffs,
how can you know the danger of falling from the summit;
if you do not approach a deep spring,
how can you know the danger of drowning;
if you do not observe the vast sea,
how can you know the danger of wind and waves.
Could the loss of things not be due to these?
If a gentleman is cautious regarding these three things,
then he will have no trouble befall him."
Zǐgòng asked Confucius, saying:
"I, Cì, am already in a subordinate position,
but I do not know the way to be subordinate,
I venture to ask."
Confucius said:
"To be subordinate,
is like the soil.
Dig deep into it, and springs will emerge;
plant the soil, and all grains will grow;
plants and trees will be planted there,
birds and beasts will be nurtured.
Living things come forth from it,
and dead things enter into it.
Accumulating merits without being conceited,
Broadening one's aspirations without being intolerant.
This is the way to serve as a subordinate."
Kǒngzǐ was going to Zhèng,
and became separated from his disciples.
He stood alone outside the east outer city gate.
Someone said to Zǐgòng,
"Outside the east gate there is a man,
who is nine feet six inches tall,
with river eyes and a prominent forehead,
his head resembles Yáo,
his neck resembles Gāo Yáo,
his shoulders resemble Zǐchǎn,
but from the waist down,
he is three inches shorter than Yǔ,
and he looks dejected like a homeless dog."
Zǐgòng told Kǒngzǐ about this.
Kǒngzǐ was delighted and sighed, saying:
"The form is a minor matter,
like a homeless dog,
is that so?
Is that so!"
Kǒngzǐ was going to Wèi,
the road led through Pú,
Gōngshū Shì used Pú to rebel against Wèi,
and (Kǒngzǐ's party) stopped him.
Among Kǒngzǐ's disciples was one named Gōngliáng Rú,
a man who was worthy and tall,
possessed of courage and strength.
With five chariots of his own,
he followed the Master on his journey,
and sighing deeply, said:
"In the past, when I followed the Master,
we encountered difficulty in Kuāng,
and again trees were cut down in Sòng.
Now we encounter difficulty here again.
Is this fate!
Rather than see the Master continually meet with difficulty,
I would prefer to fight and die."
He drew his sword and gathered a crowd,
intending to fight them.
The people of Pú, fearing, said:
"If you do not proceed to Wèi,
we will release you."
Thereupon they made a covenant with Kǒngzǐ,
and released him through the east gate.
Kǒngzǐ then went to Wèi.
Zǐgòng said:
"Can the covenant be violated?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"To demand a covenant from me is not righteous."
fēi yì yě."
The Lord of Wèi, hearing of Kǒngzǐ's arrival,
and was pleased and greeted him in the suburbs.
He asked about attacking Pú 蒲,
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 replied:
"It is permissible!"
The Duke said:
"My high officials think that Pú 蒲,
is how Wèi 衛 relies on Jìn 晉 and Chǔ 楚,
wouldn't attacking it be inappropriate?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"Their men have the will to die,
those whom we would attack
would be no more than four or five people."
The Duke said:
"Good."
In the end, they did not attack.
Another day,
Líng Gōng 靈公 again spoke with the Master,
and saw wild geese flying overhead,
and looked up at them,
with a displeased expression.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 then departed.
Wèi Qú Boyù 衛蘧伯玉 was virtuous,
but Líng Gōng 靈公 did not employ him;
Mí Zixia 彌子瑕 was unworthy,
and instead he appointed him.
Shǐ Yú repeatedly remonstrated but was not heeded.
Shǐ Yú became ill and was about to die.
He instructed his son, saying:
"I, in the court of Wèi,
was unable to promote Qū Bóyù, nor dismiss Mǐ Zǐxiá.
This is because I, as a minister, was unable to correct my ruler.
To live and be unable to correct one's ruler,
then in death, there is no way to complete the rites properly.
After I die,
place my corpse under the window,
and that will be the end of it for me."
His son followed his instructions.
Líng Gōng came to offer condolences.
He found it strange and asked about it.
His son told the Duke what his father had said.
The Duke was astonished and lost his composure,
saying:
"This is my fault."
Thereupon he ordered that the burial be held in the guest's position,
promoted Qū Bóyù and employed him,
dismissed Mǐ Zǐxiá and kept him at a distance.
Confucius heard of this
and said:
"Those who remonstrate directly in ancient times,
once they die, that is the end of it.
There has never been anyone like Shǐ Yú, who even in death remonstrated with his corpse,
and whose loyalty moved his ruler.
Can he not be called upright?"
The Virtue of the Five Emperors, Chapter Twenty-Three
Zǎi Wǒ asked Confucius, saying:
"In the past, I heard Róng Yī say:
'The Yellow Emperor lived for three hundred years.'
May I ask:
The Yellow Emperor,
was he a man?
Or was he not a man?
How could he have lived for three hundred years?"
Confucius said:
"Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, and the Duke of Zhōu,
they cannot all be observed.
And concerning your question about the Yellow Emperor of ancient times,
are you saying it is difficult for teachers to speak about it?"
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"The traditions of ancient times,
obscure sayings,
hasty collections of arguments,
unclear meanings,
if they are not the way of a gentleman,
then my question is certainly valid."
Confucius said:
"Alright.
I have vaguely heard some accounts of it.
The Yellow Emperor,
was the son of Shǎo Diǎn,
named Xuānyuán.
He was born with a divine spirit,
was able to speak while still weak,
was young yet possessed both sagacity and solemnity,
and was kind, intelligent, sincere, and trustworthy.
When he grew up, he was intelligent,
regulated the five *qì*,
established the five measures,
cared for the myriad people,
measured the four directions,
tamed oxen and rode horses,
and subdued fierce beasts.
He fought Yán Dì in the wilderness of Bǎnquán,
defeating him after three battles.
He was the first to introduce clothing,
creating the *fǔfú* (embroidered patterns on ceremonial robes),
to govern the people,
conforming to the principles of Heaven and Earth,
understanding the reasons for the hidden and the visible,
and understanding the explanations for death, survival, and destruction.
He sowed the hundred grains according to the seasons,
tasted the flavors of grasses and trees,
and his benevolence extended to birds, beasts, and insects.
He examined the sun, moon, and stars,
strained his ears and eyes,
worked hard with his mind and strength,
and used water, fire, and material resources to nurture the people.
The people relied on his benefits,
and died after a hundred years;
The people feared their spirits and perished within a hundred years;
bǎi nián ér wáng;
the people employed their teachings and changed within a hundred years.
bǎi nián ér yí.
Therefore, it is said:
"The Yellow Emperor lasted for three hundred years."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Emperor Zhuānxū?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Five Emperors used explanations,
the Three Kings had standards.
You want to hear all the accounts of the ancient past in one day,
how rash you are, Yǔ!"
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"In the past, I heard from you, Master, saying:
'Young men, do not harbor any doubts.'
Therefore, I dare to ask."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Zhuānxū was
the grandson of the Yellow Emperor,
the son of Chāngyì,
named Gāoyáng.
He was deep and had strategies,
he was unblocked and understood what was distant,
he nurtured resources to take responsibility for the land,
he followed the seasons to emulate Heaven,
he relied on ghosts and spirits to establish righteousness,
He governed the temperament and nature in order to teach the masses,
was pure and sincere in order to perform sacrifices,
and toured the four seas in order to bring peace to the people.
To the north, he reached Yōulíng,
to the south, he reached Jiāozhǐ,
to the west, he arrived at the shifting sands,
and to the east, he reached the Coiled Tree.
All kinds of movement and stillness,
things both small and great,
wherever the sun and moon shone,
nothing failed to submit to him."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Dì Kù?"
Confucius said:
"He was the grandson of Xuánxiāo,
and the son of Qiáojí,
and was called Gāoxīn.
He was born with divine qualities,
and he named himself.
He bestowed widely and profited generously,
but not for his own person.
He was intelligent and knew things far away,
he was perceptive and investigated what was subtle.
He was benevolent and had authority,
he was kind and trustworthy,
and thereby conformed to the righteousness of Heaven and Earth.
He knew what the people urgently needed,
He cultivated himself and the world submitted;
he took the resources of the land and used them sparingly;
he cherished and taught the myriad people and enlightened them with benefit;
he calculated the risings and new moons of the sun and moon and welcomed and escorted them;
he understood the spirits and reverently served them.
His countenance was harmonious;
his virtue was weighty;
his actions were timely;
his clothing was appropriate.
Spring, summer, autumn, and winter,
he nurtured and protected the world;
where the sun and moon shone,
where wind and rain reached,
nothing did not follow his transformation."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Dì Yáo?"
Confucius said:
"The son of Gāo Xīnshì,
was called Táo Táng.
His benevolence was like Heaven;
his wisdom was like the spirits;
approaching him was like the sun;
looking upon him was like the clouds.
Rich yet not arrogant,
noble yet able to be humble.
Bó Yí oversaw the rites,
Lóng Kuí oversaw the music,
Shùn served according to the times,
observed the four seasons,
endeavored to be the first to follow the ways of the early people,
exiled the Four Fiends, and the world submitted.
His words were never in error,
his virtue never wavered,
within the Four Seas,
wherever boats and carriages reached,
none did not become pacified and pleased."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Emperor Shùn?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"He was the grandson of Qiáo Niú,
the son of Gǔ Sǒu,
called Yǒu Yú.
Shùn’s filial piety and brotherly love were renowned in all directions;
he made pottery and cultivated fields to serve his parents;
he was generous and gentle,
earnest and quick-witted, and knew the times;
he revered Heaven and loved the people,
cared for those far away and treated those near with affection.
He received the Great Mandate
and relied on the two daughters [of Yáo].
He was enlightened, wise, and intelligent,
and became the Emperor of the world.
He appointed twenty-two ministers
to carry on the old duties of Yáo,
He cultivated himself.
Heaven was leveled and the earth was completed,
he patrolled and hunted in the four seas,
every five years began a new cycle.
He reigned for thirty years,
and succeeded the emperor for fifty years.
He ascended the mountains,
and died in the wilderness of Cāngwú and was buried there."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"May I ask about Yǔ?"
Confucius said:
"He was the grandson of Gāoyáng,
the son of Gǔn,
called Xià Hòu.
He was quick and diligent, able to accomplish things;
his virtue was not lacking,
his benevolence was approachable,
his words were trustworthy.
His voice was the standard of music,
his body was the standard of measurement.
Diligent and reverent,
he was the guideline and the framework.
His accomplishments made him the master of the hundred spirits,
his kindness made him the father and mother of the people.
He held the plumb line in his left hand,
and the compass and square in his right,
he followed the four seasons,
Relying on the Four Seas,
he employed Gāo Yáo and Bó Yì to assist in his governance,
and he raised his six armies to punish those who did not submit.
Within the Four Extremes,
there was no one among the people who dared not obey."
Confucius said:
"Yǔ!
The great were like Heaven,
the small were like words,
the people's joy reached its peak.
Yǔ was truly not that kind of person."
Zǎi Wǒ said:
"Yǔ was not sufficient to caution him.
I respectfully accept your command."
Another day,
Zǎi Wǒ told this to Zǐ Gòng,
and Zǐ Gòng related it to Confucius.
Confucius said:
"If I wanted to judge people by their appearance,
then I would have changed my mind about Miè Míng;
if I wanted to judge people by their words,
then I would have changed my mind about Zǎi Wǒ;
if I wanted to judge people by their countenance,
then I would have changed my mind about Zǐ Zhāng."
Zǎi Wǒ heard this and was afraid,
and did not dare to see him again.
The Twenty-Fourth: The Five Emperors.
Jì Kāngzǐ asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"I have long heard the names of the Five Emperors,
but do not know their actual reality.
May I ask, what are the Five Emperors?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In the past, Qiū heard Lǎo Dān say:
'Heaven has the Five Elements:
Wood, Fire, Metal, Water, and Earth.
They divide time and transform and nurture,
to complete the myriad things.
Their spirits are called the Five Emperors.'
The ancient kings
changed their titles with each dynastic succession,
taking the Five Elements as their model.
The Five Elements replaced each other in ruling,
beginning and ending in mutual generation,
also symbolizing their meaning.
Therefore, those who were enlightened kings
were associated with the Five Elements in death.
Thus, Tài Hào is associated with Wood,
Yándì is associated with Fire,
Huángdì is associated with Earth,
Shǎo Hào is associated with Metal,
and Zhuānxū is associated with Water."
Kāngzǐ said:
"How did Tài Hào Shì begin with Wood?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The employment of the Five Elements
begins first with Wood.
Wood is the East.
All things originate and emerge from it.
Therefore, kings model themselves on it,
and begin by ruling the world with the virtue of Wood.
After that, they follow the element that Wood generates, passing on the succession in turn."
Kāngzǐ said:
"I have heard that Gōumáng is the Minister of Wood,
Zhùróng is the Minister of Fire,
Rùshōu is the Minister of Metal,
Xuánmíng is the Minister of Water,
and Hòutǔ is the Minister of Earth.
These are the masters of the Five Elements and do not cause disorder.
Why are they also called Emperors?"
The Master said:
"All the Five Ministers
are official titles of the Five Elements.
The Five Elements assist and complete the Supreme God (Shàngdì),
and are called the Five Emperors,
with the likes of Tàihào being associated with them.
They are also called Emperors,
following their titles.
In the past, Shǎohào Shì had four uncles,
named Chóng,
Gāi,
Xiū,
and Xī.
Those who truly embodied metal, wood, and water,
made Zhòng into Gōumáng,
made Gāi into Rùshōu,
and made Xiū and Xī into Xuánmíng.
The son of Zhuānxū was named Lí,
and became Zhùróng.
The son of Gōnggōng was named Gōulóng,
and became Hòutǔ.
These five each used their respective abilities as official duties,
were high ministers when alive,
and noble gods when dead,
separately called the Five Sacrifices,
and could not be equated with the Di."
Kāngzǐ said:
"According to this account,
when emperors changed their dynastic titles,
according to the virtues of the Five Elements,
each had something they governed.
Then what events did they preside over when these elements changed?"
jiē zhǔ hé shì?"
Confucius said:
"What they valued followed the order of the virtues under which they reigned.
The Xiàhòu dynasty reigned with the virtue of metal and valued black,
for important affairs they collected at dusk,
for military affairs they rode black horses,
and for sacrifices they used black.
The Yin people used the virtue of water,
valued white,
Dà shì liǎn yòng rì zhōng, [Great matters were collected and employed at midday,]
róng shì chéng hàn, [military matters were conducted on reddish-brown horses,]
shēng yòng bái. [and sacrificial animals were white.]
Zhōu rén yǐ mù dé wáng, [The Zhōu people reigned through the virtue of wood,]
shàng chì, [and esteemed red.]
Dà shì liǎn yòng rì chū, [Great matters were collected and employed at sunrise,]
róng shì chéng yuán, [military matters were conducted on sorrel horses,]
shēng yòng xīng. [and sacrificial animals were reddish-brown.]
Cǐ sān dài zhī suǒ yǐ bù tóng. [These are the reasons why the Three Dynasties differed.]"
Kāng Zǐ yuē: [Kāngzǐ said:]
"Táng, Yú èr dì, [The two emperors, Táng and Yú,]
qí suǒ shàng zhě hé sè? [what color did they esteem?" ]
Kǒng Zǐ yuē: [Confucius said:]
"Yáo yǐ huǒ dé wáng, [Yáo reigned through the virtue of fire,]
sè shàng huáng. [and esteemed yellow.]
Shùn yǐ tǔ dé wáng, [Shùn reigned through the virtue of earth,]
sè shàng qīng. [and esteemed green/blue.]"
Kāng Zǐ yuē: [Kāngzǐ said:]
"Táo Táng, Yǒu Yú, Xià Hòu, Yīn, Zhōu dú bù dé pèi wǔ dì, [Táo Táng, Yǒu Yú, the Xià Dynasty, the Yīn Dynasty, and the Zhōu Dynasty alone could not be matched with the Five Emperors,]
yì zhě dé bù jí shàng gǔ yé? [is it perhaps that their virtue did not reach that of high antiquity?]
Jiāng yǒu xiàn hū? [Or is there a limit?" ]
Kǒng Zǐ yuē: [Confucius said:]
"Gǔ zhī píng zhì shuǐ tǔ jí bō zhí bǎi gǔ zhě zhòng yǐ, [Of those in ancient times who regulated the water and earth and sowed the hundred grains, there were many,]
wéi Gōu Lóng jiān shí yú shè, [but only Gōu Lóng also received offerings at the altars of the soil,]
ér Qì wèi Jì shén, [and Qì became the god of millet,]
yì dài fèng zhī, [each dynasty honored them,]
wú gǎn yì zhě, [and none dared add to them.]
Míng bù kě yǔ děng. [This shows that they cannot be equaled.]
Therefore, from Tài Hào 太陽 onwards,
up to Zhuān Xū 顓頊,
their reigns corresponded to the Five Elements,
the number was not merely five,
but matched the Five Emperors,
because their virtues could not be excessive."
Holding the Reins, Section Twenty-Five.
Mǐn Zǐqiān 閔子騫, serving as the governor of Fèi 費,
asked Kǒngzǐ 孔子 about governance.
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"Use virtue and law.
For virtue and law
are the tools for governing the people,
just as a horse is controlled by a bit and bridle.
The ruler is the man;
the officials are the reins;
punishments are the whip.
The governance of a ruler
lies in holding the reins and whip."
Zǐqiān 子騫 said:
"May I ask about the governance of the ancients?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"In ancient times, the Son of Heaven used the Inner Historian as his left and right hands,
used virtue and law as the bit and bridle,
used the hundred officials as the reins,
used punishments as the whip,
and used the myriad people as the horse,
thus ruling the world for hundreds of years without fail.
One who is skilled at managing horses
straightens the bit and bridle,
aligns the reins and whip,
balances the horse's strength,
harmonize the horse's heart.
Therefore, the mouth is silent and the horse responds,
the reins and whip are not raised, yet they reach a thousand *lǐ*.
Those who are good at managing the people,
unify their virtue and laws,
rectify their hundreds of officials,
in order to equalize the people's strength,
harmonize and pacify the people's hearts.
Therefore, commands are not repeated and the people obediently follow,
punishments are not used and the world is well-governed.
Therefore, Heaven and Earth are virtuous toward them,
and the millions of people cherish them.
Now, Heaven and Earth are virtuous toward them,
the millions of people cherish them,
their governance is beautiful,
and the people praise them.
Now, when people speak of the Five Emperors (*Wǔdì*) and the Three Kings (*Sānwáng*),
their prosperity is unparalleled,
their awesome influence seems to still exist,
what is the reason for this?
Their laws were flourishing,
their virtue was abundant,
Therefore, when thinking of their virtue, one must mention the person.
Pray to them morning and evening.
Their fame ascends to heaven.
Shàngdì (上帝), the Highest Divinity, altogether enjoys their offerings.
Thereby, their dynasty is perpetuated, and their years are bountiful.
Those who cannot govern the people
abandon their virtuous methods (dé fǎ 德法)
and exclusively use punishments and laws (xíng pì 刑辟).
It is like governing horses,
abandoning their bit and bridle (xián lè 衘勒) and exclusively using whips and goads (chuí cè 箠策);
that they will not be controlled can be certain.
Indeed, without bit and bridle but using whips and goads,
the horse will surely be injured,
and the cart will surely be destroyed.
Without virtuous methods but using punishments,
the people will surely scatter,
and the state will surely perish.
Governing a state without virtuous methods
means the people will lack cultivation;
if the people lack cultivation,
then they will be confused and lose their way.
Like this,
Shàngdì will certainly consider them to be disrupting the way of Heaven (tiān dào 天道).
If they disrupt the way of Heaven,
then punishments will be excessive (bào 㬥),
superiors and inferiors will flatter each other,
and no one will think of worries;
this is all because of a lack of principles (dào 道).
Nowadays, when people speak of the wicked,
they invariably compare them to Jié 桀 and Zhòu 紂.
What is the reason for this?
Their laws were not heeded,
and their virtue was not substantial.
Therefore, the people loathed their cruelty and violence,
and none did not sigh and lament.
Morning and evening they prayed about them,
their voices ascending to Heaven.
The Supreme God did not pardon them,
but sent down calamity and punishment,
disasters arose together,
thereby extinguishing their line.
Therefore, it is said:
Virtue and law
are the foundation of governing the people.
The rulers of all under Heaven in antiquity
used the Six Offices to govern everything.
The office of the Prime Minister was used to establish the Way,
the office of the Minister of Education was used to establish Virtue,
the office of the Minister of Rites was used to establish Benevolence,
the office of the Minister of War was used to establish Sagacity,
the office of the Minister of Justice was used to establish Righteousness,
and the office of the Minister of Works was used to establish Ritual.
Holding the Six Offices in hand, they were used as reins;
harmonizing and combining benevolence was used for guidance.
Therefore, it is said:
One who drives four horses holds six reins,
御天下者正六官。 The one who governs the world rectifies the six offices.
是故善御馬者， Therefore, a skilled horseman,
正身以揔轡， straightens his body to grasp the reins,
均馬力， balances the horse's strength,
齊馬心， aligns the horse's will,
廻旋曲折， turns and twists,
唯其所之， going wherever he wants it to go,
故可以取長道， therefore can travel long distances,
可赴急疾， and can rush swiftly.
此聖人所以御天地與人事之法則也。 This is the principle by which sages govern heaven and earth and human affairs.
天子以內史為左右手， The Son of Heaven uses the Nèishǐ (Inner Scribe) as his left and right hands,
以六官為轡已， and the six offices as the reins.
而天子與三公為執六官， The Son of Heaven together with the Three Dukes are those who hold the six offices,
均五教， balancing the five teachings,
齊五法， aligning the five laws,
故亦唯其所引， therefore also, wherever they guide,
無不如志。 nothing is not as desired.
以之道， If they use it for the Way (Dào),
則國治； then the state is well-governed;
以之德， if they use it for Virtue (Dé),
則國安； then the state is secure;
以之仁， if they use it for Benevolence (Rén),
則國和； then the state is harmonious;
以之聖， if they use it for Sagacity (Shèng),
則國平； then the state is peaceful;
以之禮， if they use it for Ritual (Lǐ),
則國定； then the state is stable;
以之義， if they use it for Righteousness (Yì),
then the state will be righteous.
This is the art of governing.
Mistakes
are something everyone is subject to.
To err and correct oneself
is called not erring.
Therefore, when subordinates are not managed,
duties are not clearly defined,
laws and ordinances are inconsistent,
and all affairs lack order,
it is called chaos.
In times of chaos, the *zhǒng zǎi* (總宰) should be reprimanded.
When the land is not cultivated,
wealth and goods do not increase,
the people are hungry and cold,
teachings are not put into practice,
customs are licentious and depraved,
and the people are scattered and dispersed,
it is called danger.
In times of danger, the *sī tú* (司徒) should be reprimanded.
When fathers and sons are not close,
elders and juniors lack order,
and the ruler and his ministers, superiors and inferiors,
are disobedient and have different aims,
it is called disharmony.
In times of disharmony, the *zōng bó* (宗伯) should be reprimanded.
When the virtuous and capable lose office and rank,
meritorious service loses reward and emolument,
The soldiers and officers are sick with resentment,
the army is weak and unusable;
this is called "unjust treatment."
With unjust treatment, then correct the Sīmǎ (司馬, Minister of War).
Punishments are cruel and disordered,
the wicked and depraved are not overcome;
this is called "unrighteousness."
With unrighteousness, then correct the Sīkòu (司寇, Minister of Justice).
Measures and standards are not accurate,
actions are unreasonable,
cities and towns are not maintained,
wealth and goods are misplaced;
this is called "poverty."
With poverty, then correct the Sīkōng (司空, Minister of Works/Agriculture).
Therefore, drivers all use the same carts and horses,
but some can travel a thousand *lǐ*,
while others cannot even reach several hundred *lǐ*;
the differences lie in their handling of advance, retreat, slowness, and speed.
Likewise, those who govern all use the same laws,
but some bring about peace,
while others bring about chaos;
the differences also lie in their handling of advance, retreat, slowness, and speed.
In ancient times,
the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ, 天子) would always, in the last month of winter, examine virtue and correct the laws,
in order to observe governance and disorder.
When virtue is flourishing, there is good governance.
When virtue is weak, there is disorder.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven examines virtue,
then the governance and disorder of the world,
can be known while sitting above the ancestral hall.
Truly, if virtue flourishes, then the laws are refined;
if virtue does not flourish, then even refining the laws and government,
it cannot prevent decline.
Therefore, it is said:
"The ruler again, in early spring, evaluates the virtue and ability of officials.
Those who understand virtuous laws are considered virtuous;
those who can implement virtuous laws are considered to have conduct;
those who can accomplish virtuous laws are considered to have merit;
those who can govern with virtuous laws are considered to have wisdom.
Therefore, when the Son of Heaven evaluates officials, virtuous laws are implemented,
affairs are governed, and merits are achieved.
In the last month of winter, laws are rectified;
in early spring, officials are evaluated;
these are the essentials of governing a state."
Zǐ Xià asked Confucius, saying:
"Shāng has heard that the *Yì* (Book of Changes) produces people,
as well as the myriad things, birds, beasts, and insects,
each having odd and even numbers,
their *qì* (vital energy) being different,
and ordinary people do not know the reality of it.
Only those who understand the Dao and virtue can trace it to its origin.
Heaven is one,
Earth is two,
man is three,
three times three is like nine,
nine times nine is eighty-one.
One governs the sun,
the number of the sun is ten,
therefore humans are born in the tenth month.
Eight times nine is seventy-two,
even numbers follow odd numbers;
odd numbers govern *chén*;
*chén* governs the month;
the month governs the horse;
therefore, horses are born in the twelfth month.
Seven times nine is sixty-three;
three governs the Dipper (*dǒu*);
the Dipper governs the dog;
therefore, dogs are born in the third month.
Six times nine is fifty-four;
four governs the time;
the time governs the pig (*shǐ*);
therefore, pigs are born in the fourth month.
Five times nine is forty-five;
the tone governs the monkey (*yuán*);
therefore, monkeys are born in the fifth month.
Four times nine is thirty-six;
six governs the pitch-pipe (*lǜ*);
the pitch-pipe governs the deer;
therefore, deer are born in the sixth month.
Three times nine is twenty-seven;
Seven are the master stars.
The star masters the tiger,
therefore tigers are born in the seventh month.
Two nines are eighteen,
eight governs the wind,
the wind governs the insects,
five governs the tone;
therefore insects are born in the eighth month.
The rest each follow their own kind.
Birds and fish are born of yin,
but belong to yang,
therefore they are all born from eggs.
Fish swim in water,
birds fly in the clouds,
therefore at the start of winter, swallows and sparrows enter the sea and transform into clams.
Silkworms eat but do not drink,
cicadas drink but do not eat,
mayflies neither drink nor eat,
this is why all things are different.
Creatures with shells and scales eat in summer and hibernate in winter,
those who gnaw and swallow have eight orifices and are born as beasts,
those who have interlocking teeth have nine orifices and are born viviparously,
those with four legs have no feathers or wings,
those with horns have no upper teeth,
those without horns and without front teeth produce fat,
those with horns and without teeth produce grease,
those born during the day resemble the father,
those born at night resemble the mother,
therefore the utmost yin governs the female,
"Supreme Yang governs the female."
May I venture to ask, is that so?"
Confucius said:
"It is so.
I once heard Lǎodān say the same as you."
Zǐxià said:
"Shāng heard in the *Book of Mountains*:
East and west of the earth are called latitudes,
north and south are called longitudes;
mountains accumulate virtue,
rivers accumulate punishment;
the high are associated with life,
the low are associated with death;
hills and mounds are female,
valleys and ravines are female;
oysters, clams, turtles, pearls, along with the sun and moon, have periods of fullness and emptiness.
Therefore, people of hard soil are strong,
people of soft soil are gentle,
people of barren soil are large,
people of sandy soil are delicate,
people of fertile soil are beautiful,
people of depleted soil are ugly.
Those who eat water are good swimmers and tolerate cold,
those who eat earth are mindless and unceasing,
those who eat wood are strong but unruly,
those who eat grass are good runners but foolish,
those who eat mulberry have order but become moths,
those who eat meat are brave and defend,
Shí qì zhě shénmíng ér shòu,
Those who eat grains possess wisdom and skill.
Those who do not eat will neither die nor become divine.
Therefore, it is said:
Of the three hundred and sixty kinds of feathered insects,
the phoenix is their chief;
of the three hundred and sixty kinds of hairy insects,
the *lín* (scaled dragon-like creature) is their chief;
of the three hundred and sixty kinds of shelled insects,
the turtle is their chief;
of the three hundred and sixty kinds of scaled insects,
the dragon is their chief;
of the three hundred and sixty kinds of naked insects,
humans are their chief.
This is the beauty of heaven and earth,
the variety of different shapes and kinds.
A ruler's actions must accord with the Dao,
and their stillness must accord with principle,
in order to serve the nature of heaven and earth,
and not harm that which they govern;
this is called benevolence and sagacity."
Zǐ Xià finished speaking and departed.
Zǐ Gòng stepped forward and said,
"What do you think of Shāng's discussion?"
Kǒngzǐ said,
"What do you think?"
He replied,
"It is subtle, truly subtle,
ránzé fēi zhìshì zhī dài yě. " Therefore, it is not what a well-governed world awaits."
Kǒngzǐ yuē: Confucius said:
"Rán, "Yes,
gè qí suǒ néng. " each according to their ability."
Běnmìng Jiě Dì Èrshíliù Chapter 26: Explanation of Innate Destiny
Lǔ Āigōng wèn yú Kǒngzǐ yuē: Lǔ Āigōng asked Confucius, saying:
"Rén zhī mìng yǔ xìng héwèi yě? " "What is meant by a person's *mìng* (destiny) and *xìng* (nature)?"
Kǒngzǐ duì yuē: Confucius answered, saying:
"Fēn yú dào, "That which is apportioned from the Dao,
wèi zhī mìng; is called *mìng* (destiny);
xíng yú yī, that which takes form in the One,
wèi zhī xìng; is called *xìng* (nature);
huà yú yīnyáng, that which transforms through Yin and Yang,
xiàng xíng ér fā, that takes form and emerges,
wèi zhī shēng; is called *shēng* (life);
huà qióng shù jìn, when transformation reaches its limit and the number is exhausted,
wèi zhī sǐ. it is called *sǐ* (death).
Gù mìng zhě, Therefore, *mìng* (destiny)
xìng zhī shǐ yě; is the beginning of *xìng* (nature);
sǐ zhě, *sǐ* (death)
shēng zhī zhōng yě. is the end of *shēng* (life).
Yǒu shǐ zé bì yǒu zhōng yǐ. If there is a beginning, then there must be an end.
Rén shǐ shēng ér yǒu bù jù zhě wǔ yān, When a person is first born, there are five things they do not possess:
mù wú jiàn, the eyes cannot see,
bù néng shí, cannot eat,
bù néng xíng, cannot walk,
Cannot speak,
cannot transform.
When three months old, there is a slight warmth,
then there is sight;
at eight months, teeth grow,
then able to eat;
at three years the fontanelle closes,
then able to speak;
at sixteen years, the essence flows,
then able to transform.
When Yin reaches its limit, it reverts to Yang,
therefore Yin changes by Yang;
when Yang reaches its limit, it reverts to Yin,
therefore Yang transforms by Yin.
Therefore, a male child grows teeth at eight months,
and loses his milk teeth at eight years.
A female child grows teeth at seven months,
and loses her milk teeth at seven years,
and transforms at fourteen.
One Yang and one Yin,
odd and even are matched,
then the Dao combines and transformation is accomplished.
The beginnings of nature and life
are formed here."
The Duke said:
"A male at sixteen has flowing essence,
a female transforms at fourteen,
then they can produce people.
And according to ritual, men must be thirty before they have a household,
and women must be twenty before they have a husband.
Isn't that late?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The ritual speaks of the extreme, but it is not excessive.
A man is capped at twenty,
having the beginning of being a father;
a woman is permitted to marry at fifteen,
having the way of going to someone.
Proceeding from this point,
then they marry themselves.
All living things close and hide in the yin,
and it is the beginning of transformation and nurturing.
Therefore, the sage follows the time to unite couples.
Men exhaust the heavenly numbers.
When frost falls, women's work is completed,
and the marrying woman departs.
When the ice melts, farming and sericulture begin,
and marriage rites are determined at this time.
Men,
are those who take on the way of heaven and nurture the myriad things.
Knowing what can be done,
knowing what cannot be done;
knowing what can be said,
knowing what cannot be said;
knowing what can be done,
knowing what cannot be done.
Therefore, examining their relationships and clarifying their distinctions,
This is called knowledge,
and it is what the conduct of a common man models.
Women,
are those who follow the teachings of men and cultivate their principles.
Therefore, they do not have the right to make their own decisions,
but must follow the Way of the Three Obediences:
in youth, they obey their father and elder brothers;
after marriage, they obey their husband;
after the husband's death, they obey their son;
meaning there is no thought of remarriage;
directives and orders do not come from their private chambers;
their duty lies in providing food and drink;
they do not engage in improper conduct outside the threshold;
they do not cross borders to attend funerals;
they do not act without authorization;
they do not succeed on their own;
they act only after consultation;
they speak only after verification;
they do not stroll in the courtyard during the day;
they use a light when walking at night;
this is what the virtue of a common woman models."
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 then said,
"There are five types of women not to be taken:
those who disobey their family;
those who disrupt their family;
those from families with hereditary criminals;
those with vile diseases;
and those who are the eldest daughter after losing their father.
婦有七出、三不去；fù yǒu qī chū, sān bù qù; A wife can be divorced for seven reasons, but there are three cases where she cannot be divorced.
七出者：qī chū zhě: The seven reasons for divorce are:
不順父母出者，bù shùn fùmǔ chū zhě, Disobeying parents-in-law;
無子者，wú zǐ zhě, Not bearing a son;
婬僻者，yín pì zhě, Being adulterous;
嫉妬者，jí dù zhě, Being jealous;
惡疾者，è jí zhě, Having a loathsome disease;
多口舌者，duō kǒushé zhě, Being gossipy and argumentative;
竊盜者。qiè dào zhě. Committing theft.
三不去者：sān bù qù zhě: The three cases where she cannot be divorced are:
謂有所取無所歸一也，wèi yǒu suǒ qǔ wú suǒ guī yī yě, When she has nowhere else to return to (no family to go back to);
與共更三年之喪二也，yǔ gòng gēng sān nián zhī sāng èr yě, When she has observed the three-year mourning period for the deceased parents-in-law alongside her husband;
先貧賤後富貴者三也。xiān pínjiàn hòu fùguì zhě sān yě. When the husband was poor and lowly at the time of marriage, but later became rich and noble.
凡此聖人所以順男女之際，fán cǐ shèngrén suǒyǐ shùn nánnǚ zhī jì, All of these are the ways in which the sages harmonized the relationship between men and women,
重婚姻之始也。」zhòng hūnyīn zhī shǐ yě." and valued the beginning of marriage."
孔子曰：「Kǒngzǐ yuē: Confucius said:
禮之所以象五行也，lǐ zhī suǒyǐ xiàng wǔxíng yě, "The rites are patterned after the Five Elements;
其義、四時也，qí yì, sìshí yě, their meaning is like the Four Seasons.
故喪禮有舉焉。gù sānglǐ yǒu jǔ yān. Therefore, funeral rites have their procedures.
有恩有義，yǒu ēn yǒu yì, There is kindness and there is righteousness;
有節有權，yǒu jié yǒu quán, there is regulation and there is expediency.
其恩厚者其服重。qí ēn hòu zhě qí fú zhòng. Those with deep kindness have heavy mourning garments.
故為父母斬衰三年，gù wèi fùmǔ zhǎncuī sān nián, Therefore, one wears coarse mourning for three years for parents;
以恩制者也。yǐ ēn zhì zhě yě. this is regulated by kindness.
門內之治恩掩義，mén nèi zhī zhì ēn yǎn yì, In the governance within the household, kindness overshadows righteousness;
門外之治義掩恩。mén wài zhī zhì yì yǎn ēn. in the governance outside the household, righteousness overshadows kindness.
Serve the ruler as you serve your father,
and reverence is the same.
Valuing the valued and honoring the honored,
this is the greatest of righteousness.
Therefore, to mourn for a ruler, one also wears mourning garments for three years,
which is governed by righteousness.
Bathe every three days,
wash hair every three months,
change to finer mourning clothes after a year,
injury should not destroy one's nature,
do not injure the living because of the dead,
mourning should not exceed three years,
coarse mourning clothes should not be mended,
the tomb should not be overly repaired,
on the day of removing mourning clothes, play a plain zither,
showing the people that there is an end (to mourning).
All of this is to control (mourning) with regulation.
Serve the mother as you serve your father,
and love is the same.
Heaven has no two suns,
a state has no two rulers,
a family has no two honored ones,
this is how to govern.
Therefore, when the father is alive, mourning for the mother is for one year wearing *zīcuī*,
showing that there are not two honored ones.
When all the officials are prepared,
all things are ready,
and affairs are carried out without speaking,
Fú ér qǐ; (Supporting them) to rise;
yán ér hòu shì xíng zhě, (Those who) speak and then affairs are conducted,
zhàng ér qǐ; (support themselves with a) cane to rise;
shēn zì zhí shì xíng zhě, (Those who) personally handle affairs,
miàn gòu ér yǐ; (their) faces are merely dirty;
cǐ yǐ quán zhì zhě yě. This is how authority is used to control (them).
Qīn shǐ sǐ, When a parent first dies,
sān rì bù dài, (one is) not idle for three days,
sān yuè bù xiè, (one is) not lax for three months,
jī bēi háo, (for) a year, (one) grieves and wails,
sān nián yōu, (for) three years, (one) sorrows,
āi zhī shā yě. This is the diminishing of grief.
Shèngrén yīn shā yǐ zhì jié yě." The sage uses this diminishing to regulate (mourning) observances."
Lún Lǐ Dì Èrshíqī Discussion of Ritual, Chapter Twenty-Seven
Kǒngzǐ xiánjū, Kǒngzǐ was at leisure,
Zǐ Zhāng, Zǐ Gòng, Yán Yóu shì. Zǐ Zhāng, Zǐ Gòng, and Yán Yóu were in attendance.
Lùn jí yú lǐ, Discussing ritual,
Kǒngzǐ yuē: Kǒngzǐ said:
"Jū! "Sit!
Rǔ sān rén zhě. You three.
Wú yǔ rǔ yǐ lǐ zhōu liú wú bù biàn yě." I will tell you about ritual, which flows everywhere without omission."
Zǐ Gòng yuè xí ér duì yuē: Zǐ Gòng moved off his mat and replied:
"Gǎn wèn rúhé?" "May I venture to ask how?"
Zǐ yuē: Kǒngzǐ said:
"Jìng ér bù zhōng lǐ, "Respectful but not in accordance with ritual
wèi zhī yě; is called rudeness;
To be respectful without conforming to ritual is called obsequiousness;
to be brave without conforming to ritual
is called rebelliousness."
The Master said:
"Obsequiousness steals away kindness and benevolence."
Zǐ Gòng said:
"May I venture to ask what is meant by conforming to ritual?"
The Master said:
"Ritual!
Ritual is the means by which moderation is achieved."
Zǐ Gòng withdrew.
Yán Yóu stepped forward and said:
"May I venture to ask, does ritual
embrace evil while preserving the good?"
The Master said:
"It does."
Zǐ Gòng asked:
"What is meant by this?"
The Master said:
"The rites of the suburban and ancestral altars
are for showing kindness to ghosts and spirits;
the rites of the *dì* and *cháng* sacrifices
are for showing kindness to the ancestral order;
the rites of providing offerings
are for showing kindness to the dead and mourning;
the rites of archery feasts
are for showing kindness to the local community;
The rites of feasting and entertainment
are how one treats guests with benevolence.
Understanding the meaning of suburban sacrifices and the rites of dì and cháng sacrifices,
governing a state will be as easy as pointing at one's palm.
Therefore, by applying them at home, one possesses propriety,
and thus elders and juniors are distinguished.
By applying them within the inner chambers, one possesses propriety,
and thus the three kinship groups are harmonious.
By applying them in the court, one possesses propriety,
and thus official ranks are ordered.
By applying them in hunting, one possesses propriety,
and thus military affairs are practiced.
By applying them in the military, one possesses propriety,
and thus military achievements are accomplished.
Therefore, palaces obtain their proper dimensions,
cauldrons and sacrificial vessels obtain their proper forms,
things obtain their proper timing,
music obtains its proper rhythm,
carriages obtain their proper crossbars,
spirits obtain their proper offerings,
mourning rites obtain their proper sorrow,
debates obtain their proper sides,
all officials obtain their proper roles,
and governmental affairs obtain their proper implementation.
Added to oneself and placed before,
all the actions of the masses
will attain their appropriateness."
Yán Yóu retreated.
Zǐ Zhāng stepped forward and asked:
"May I venture to ask, what is meant by 'rites'?"
The Master said:
"Rites,
are the ordering of affairs.
When a gentleman has affairs,
he must have order.
Governing a state without rites,
is like a blind man without a guide,
wandering aimlessly, where can he go?
It is like seeking something in a dark room in the middle of the night,
how can one see without a candle?
Therefore, without rites, hands and feet have nowhere to be placed,
eyes and ears have nothing to add,
advancing, retreating, bowing, and yielding have no regulation.
Therefore, in their dwellings,
the elder and the young lose their distinction,
within the household and amongst the three kinship groups, harmony is lost,
in the court, official positions and ranks lose their order,
in hunting and military matters, strategies are lost,
in armies, the strategic advantage is lost,
palaces lose their standards,
sacrificial vessels lose their form,
things lose their timing,
music loses its rhythm,
carriages lose their rails,
spirits lose their offerings,
funerals lose their sorrow,
If arguments lose their following,
if the hundred officials lose their proper form,
if government affairs lose their implementation,
if things are added to oneself and placed before (others),
if the actions of the common people lose their appropriateness,
then there is no way to hold ancestral sacrifices for the whole world."
The Master said:
"Listen carefully!
You three.
I will tell you.
Ritual still has nine aspects,
great banquets have four aspects.
If one knows this,
even if one is in the fields,
and practices it,
one is a sage.
When two rulers meet,
they yield and enter the gate,
after entering the gate, the bells are hung;
they yield and ascend the hall,
after ascending the hall, the music ends;
below, the pipes imitate dances,
the Xia flutes rise in order,
arranging the presented food vessels,
ordering the rites and music,
preparing the hundred officials,
only then do gentlemen know benevolence.
Walking conforms to the compass,
Turning follows the square;
the bells and chimes are in accordance with the correct tempo;
the guests come from Yong;
the ceremony concludes with the fluttering of feathers.
Therefore, a gentleman finds nothing that is not within ritual.
Upon entering the gate, the metal instruments sound,
showing emotion;
ascending to sing the "Qīng Miào" hymn,
showing virtue;
below, the pipes imitate the dances,
showing the affairs.
The gentlemen of old
did not necessarily speak to each other personally,
but simply showed each other ritual and music.
Now, ritual is principle;
music is modulation.
Without principle, there is no movement;
without modulation, there is no action.
To be incapable of poetry
is to be mistaken in ritual;
to be incapable of music
is to be plain in ritual;
to be deficient in virtue
is to be empty in ritual."
Zǐ Gòng arose and asked,
"In that case, was Kuí at an end?"
The Master said,
"A man of old?
These were the people of high antiquity.
To be versed in ritual but not versed in music
is called being plain;
to be versed in music but not versed in ritual
is called being biased.
Now, Kuí was versed in music but not versed in ritual,
and that is why this reputation was passed down.
These were the people of high antiquity.
All institutions are contained in ritual,
and ornamentation is contained in ritual,
but their implementation depends on people!"
The three disciples, having heard this discourse from the Master,
were suddenly enlightened, as if awakened from a dream.
Zǐxià was sitting in attendance on Confucius,
and said:
"May I ask, the *Book of Odes* says:
'The kind and gentle ruler
is the father and mother of the people.'
How can one be called the father and mother of the people?"
Confucius said:
"To be the father and mother of the people,
one must be versed in the sources of ritual and music,
so as to achieve the 'Five Attainments' and practice the 'Three Absence of Excess',
and thus move unimpeded throughout the world.
If there is failure in the four directions,
one must be the first to know it.
This is what is meant by the parents of the people."
Zǐ Xià 子夏 said:
"May I venture to ask what are the Five Arrivals?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"Where the intention (zhì) arrives,
the *Shī* 詩 (poetry) also arrives;
where the *Shī* 詩 arrives,
propriety (lǐ 禮) also arrives;
where propriety (lǐ 禮) arrives,
music (yuè 樂) also arrives;
where music (yuè 樂) arrives,
sorrow (āi 哀) also arrives.
The *Shī* 詩 and propriety (lǐ 禮) complement each other;
sorrow (āi 哀) and music (yuè 樂) give rise to each other;
therefore, if you focus your eyes and look at it directly,
you cannot possibly see it;
if you incline your ear and listen to it,
you cannot possibly hear it.
The ambition and spirit fill the space between Heaven and Earth;
their conduct fills the four seas.
This is what is meant by the Five Arrivals."
Zǐ Xià 子夏 said:
"May I venture to ask what are the Three Nothings?"
Kǒngzǐ 孔子 said:
"Music without sound,
propriety without form,
mourning without garments,
these are what is meant by the Three Nothings."
Zixia said:
"May I ask about the 'three withouts'?
Which poems are close to them?"
Confucius said:
"'Morning and night, lay the foundation of the mandate in secret,'
that is music without sound;
'Dignified deportment, stately and grand,
is not to be chosen,'
that is ritual without form;
'When the common people have mourning,
prostrate yourselves and assist them,'
that is mourning without garments."
Zixia said:
"The words are beautiful and grand!
Is that all that can be said about it?"
Confucius said:
"What do you mean by that!
I will tell you,
its meaning can still be expanded in five ways."
Zixia said:
"How so?"
Confucius said:
"Music without sound:
the *qi* arrives without deviation;
Ritual without form:
dignified deportment is slow and deliberate;
Mourning without garments:
inwardly, there is sincere sorrow;
The music without sound,
All desires are certainly fulfilled;
The ritual without form,
Superiors and inferiors are in harmony and agreement;
The mourning without mourning garments,
Extends to all nations.
If this is the case,
And furthermore, to serve them with the three impartials, and toil for the world,
This is called the Five Risings."
Zǐ Xià said:
"What are the three impartials?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Heaven impartially covers,
Earth impartially supports,
The sun and moon impartially illuminate.
It is said in the *Book of Poetry*:
'The Lord's commands are not disobeyed,
Reaching Tāng in their completeness.
Tāng's descent was not slow,
Reverent and sage, he daily ascended.
Clearly arriving slowly,
He reverently served God.'
'The Lord's commands regulated the nine regions.'
This is the virtue of Tāng."
Zǐ Xià jolted and stood up,
Leaning against the wall,
Said:
"How dare this disciple not remember it?"
Observing the Village Archery Competition, Chapter Twenty-Eight
Confucius watched the village archery competition,
and sighed,
"Archery is done for enjoyment.
How does one shoot?
How does one listen?
To release the arrow following the sound,
and not miss the target,
is only something a virtuous person can do!
As for an unworthy person,
how could they expect to get a drink?
The *Book of Poetry* says:

Suburban Sacrifices, Chapter Twenty-Nine
Duke Ding asked Confucius, saying:

Confucius replied, saying:
"The myriad things are rooted in Heaven,
and man is rooted in his ancestors.
therefore they are not the same."
The Duke said:
"What does it mean to speak of the suburban sacrifice?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"To build a mound in the south
is how one approaches the position of yang.
It is in the suburbs,
therefore it is called a suburban sacrifice."
He said:
"What are the sacrificial victims and vessels like?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The horns of the ox for the Supreme God are like cocoons and chestnuts,
and they must be purified for three months.
The ox for Hòujì is simply complete,
and that is how one distinguishes the service of the spirits of Heaven from the ghosts of men.
The sacrificial victim is red,
esteemed for the color red.
A calf is used,
esteemed for sincerity.
To sweep the ground and sacrifice is
to esteem its natural quality.
Vessels of pottery and gourds are used
to symbolize the nature of Heaven and Earth.
There is nothing among all things that can be used to express them fully,
so one relies on their natural form."
The Duke said:
"The suburban sacrifice of the Son of Heaven,
