Kǒngzǐ replied, saying:
"I have heard that the Son of Heaven divines for the suburban sacrifice.
he receives the mandate in the ancestral temple,
and prepares the tortoise shell in the shrine of the deceased father,
this is to honor the ancestors and show affection for the deceased father.
On the day of divination,
the king personally stands in the Ze Palace,
to hear the oath,
this is to receive instruction and admonishment.
After the divination,
the result is presented inside the gate of the treasury,
this is to warn all the officials.
When about to perform the suburban sacrifice,
the Son of Heaven is presented with a leather cap to hear the report,
this is to show the people the strictness of superiors.
On the day of the suburban sacrifice,
those in mourning do not dare to weep,
those wearing mourning garments do not dare to enter the city gate,
a broad sweep cleans the roads,
those walking all stop,
without orders, the people obey,
this is the height of respect.
The Son of Heaven wears a great fur coat embroidered with axes,
wearing the fur coat symbolizes Heaven,
rides in a plain cart,
valuing its simplicity.
The banner has twelve streamers,
adorned with dragons and setting forth the sun and moon,
Therefore, it imitates Heaven.
Once having arrived at the Tai Altar,
the king takes off his fur robe,
and puts on his ceremonial robe to approach the burning pyre,
wearing a crown with twelve tassels,
this is according to the numbers of Heaven.
Your servant has heard it said:
Reciting the three hundred 《Odes》,
is not sufficient for one offering;
the rites of one offering,
are not sufficient for a great feast;
the rites of a great feast,
are not sufficient for a grand military campaign;
once a grand military campaign is prepared,
it is not sufficient to feast the Emperor.
Therefore, a gentleman dares not lightly discuss rites."
Explanation of the Five Punishments, Thirtieth
Rǎn Yǒu asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"In ancient times, the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors did not use the five punishments,
is this true?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The prevention instituted by the sages,
values its being unviolated;
establishing the five punishments, yet not using them,
is how perfect governance is achieved.
All people who commit treachery, theft, disregard the law, and act recklessly,
Poverty arises from insufficiency,
and insufficiency arises from lack of measure.
With a lack of measure,
the small steal and are lazy,
the great are extravagant and wasteful,
each not knowing moderation.
Therefore, if the ruler has established systems and regulations,
then the people will know where to stop,
and if the people know where to stop, then they will not transgress.
Therefore, although there may be trials for traitors, thieves, lawbreakers, and those acting recklessly,
there will be no people trapped by punishment.
Lack of filial piety arises from unkindness,
and unkindness arises from neglecting the rites of mourning and sacrifice.
Clarifying the rites of mourning and sacrifice
is how to teach benevolence and love.
If one can achieve benevolence and love,
then they will cherish the memory of the departed in mourning.
Sacrifices will not obscure the way a son should provide for his parents.
If the rites of mourning and sacrifice are clear,
then the people will be filial.
Therefore, although there may be trials for lack of filial piety,
there will be no people trapped by punishment.
Killing one's superior arises from lack of righteousness.
Righteousness is how to distinguish the noble from the base,
and to make clear the respect due to superiors and elders.
If the noble and the base are distinguished,
and superiors and inferiors have their proper order,
then the people will all respect their superiors and revere their elders.
The rites of court visits and diplomatic missions are
the means by which righteousness is made clear.
If righteousness is necessarily made clear,
then the people will not transgress.
Therefore, although there are cases of killing superiors,
there will be no people entrapped by punishment.
Quarrels and altercations arise from mutual disrespect;
mutual disrespect arises from the lack of order between elders and juniors and the abandoning of reverence and yielding.
The rite of village drinking ceremony is
the means by which the order between elders and juniors is made clear and reverence and yielding are promoted.
If the order between elders and juniors is necessarily maintained,
the people will cherish reverence and yielding.
Therefore, although there are cases of altercation and fighting,
there will be no people entrapped by punishment.
Promiscuity and disorder arise from the lack of distinction between men and women;
if there is no distinction between men and women,
then husbands and wives will lose their proper relationship.
Marriages, betrothals, and offerings are
the means by which men and women are distinguished and the proper relationship between husband and wife is made clear.
Once men and women are distinguished,
and the relationship between husband and wife is made clear,
therefore, although there are cases of promiscuity and disorder,
there will be no people entrapped by punishment.
These five are what punishments arise from,
each having its own source.
Not to preemptively block their sources,
but instead to immediately bind them with punishments,
this is called setting traps for the people and causing them to fall into them.
The source of punishment
arises from desires and cravings being unrestrained.
Now, rites and standards are
the means by which the people's desires and cravings are controlled and likes and dislikes are made clear,
conforming to the Way of Heaven.
Once rites and standards are set forth,
and the five teachings are all cultivated,
if the people are still not transformed,
then one must clearly set forth the laws
to strengthen and secure them.
For those who commit crimes of treachery and wickedness, defiance of the law, and reckless behavior,
then regulate the measures and standards;
for those who commit crimes of unfilial piety,
then regulate the rites of mourning and sacrifice;
for those who commit crimes of killing their superiors,
then regulate the rites of court audiences;
for those who commit crimes of fighting and causing disturbances,
then regulate the rites of the village drinking ceremony;
for those who commit crimes of licentiousness and disorder,
then regulate the rites of marriage and betrothal.
This is how the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors transformed the people.
Even if there is the use of the five punishments,
is it not acceptable?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"There are five great crimes,
and killing a person is the least.
Those who defy Heaven and Earth, their crime extends to five generations;
those who falsely accuse Wén and Wǔ, their crime extends to four generations;
those who defy human relationships, their crime extends to three generations;
Those who plot with ghosts and spirits have their crimes extended to two generations.
Those who personally commit murder, the crime stops with their own person.
Therefore it is said:
"There are five major crimes,
and murder is the least of them."

What are the Four Auspicious Creatures?
Lín (麒麟), Fèng (鳳凰), Guī (龜), and Lóng (龍),

The king was in the center,

Now, ritual must be rooted in the Great One (tàiyī),

It is like wine that has yeast.

Ode to the Capping Ceremony, thirty-third
After Zhū Yǐngōng ascended the throne,
he was about to undergo the capping ceremony.
He sent a minister through Mèng Yìzǐ to ask Kǒngzǐ about the rites.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The rites should be like the capping ceremony of an heir apparent.
Capping at the eastern steps
is to signify succession.
Toasting at the guest's position
adds to his accomplishments,
three additions increase respect,
guiding and expressing his aspirations.
Bestowing a courtesy name after capping
shows respect for his name.
Even the emperor's eldest son
is still a scholar.
The rituals involved in it are unchanging,
because in all the world, no one is born noble.
The capping ceremony must be performed in the ancestral temple,
and it is conducted using the ritual of libation offerings,
with music played on metal and stone instruments to mark the rhythm;
this is how one humbles oneself to honor the ancestors,
showing that one dares not act presumptuously.
Yì Zǐ said:
"If the Son of Heaven ascends the throne without being capped,
then when he matures, that is also capping."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"In ancient times,
even if the King's heir was young,
upon ascending the throne, he was honored as the ruler.
A ruler who governs the affairs of adults,
what need does he have for capping?"
Yì Zǐ said:
"In that case, is the capping ceremony of the feudal lords different from that of the Son of Heaven?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the lord dies and the heir presides over the mourning rites,
that is also considered capping.
There is no difference for a ruler."
Yì Zǐ said:
"Is the capping ceremony of the Lord of Zhū today contrary to ritual?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The feudal lords having capping ceremonies
began in the late Xia dynasty,
and it has been passed down since then.
Now, there is no faultfinding about it.
As for the capping of the Son of Heaven:
When Wǔ Wáng 武王 died,
Chéng Wáng 成王 was thirteen years old when he succeeded to the throne.
Zhōu Gōng 周公 held the office of chief minister,
and administered the empire as regent.
The following year, in the sixth month of summer,
after the funeral rites were completed,
he capped Chéng Wáng 成王 and held court in the ancestral temple,
in order to be seen by the feudal lords,
to demonstrate that there was a ruler.
Zhōu Gōng 周公 ordered Zhù Yōng 祝雍 to compose a eulogy,
saying:
"Pray that the king becomes accomplished and not remain youthful."
Zhù Yōng 祝雍 replied:
"May the king be close to the people,
distant from indulgence,
frugal with time,
generous with wealth,
be close to the virtuous and entrust tasks to the capable."
His eulogy said:
"On this auspicious day of a fine month,
the king begins to wear the headgear of adulthood.
Put away the youthful inclinations of the king,
be wholeheartedly devoted to your duties,
revere the vast Heaven,
take the six directions as your model,
follow your ancestors,
"Eternally and without end."
"This is the system established by the Duke of Zhōu."
Yì Zǐ said:
"The capping ceremony of the feudal lords,
what is the reason for the distinction between guest and host?"
Kǒng Zǐ said:
"When a duke caps someone, he takes a minister as the guest.
Without an assistant.
The duke himself acts as the host.
He greets the guest with a bow,
ascends from the eastern steps,
and stands north of the mat.
The offering of sweet wine,
is like that for a scholar.
He treats him with the three-times-presenting ritual.
After the offering of sweet wine,
he descends from the eastern steps.
If feudal lords are not dukes but act as the host themselves,
the differences are:
they all descend from the western steps.
The dark formal robe and the leather cap are different.
The court robe is plain silk.
The duke's capping ceremony involves four additions.
He sacrifices wearing a dark coronet.
When he rewards the guest with gifts,
it is a bundle of silk and a carriage and horses.
The capping ceremony of the king's heir and other sons is similar,
with the son of Heaven acting as the host himself.
The rites for them are no different from those for the *shi* (officers);
they are entertained as guests at meals;
everything is the same."
Yìzǐ said:
"At the start of capping, one must add a black cloth cap,
why is that?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It shows that we have not lost antiquity.
In high antiquity, they wore cloth caps,
and when fasting they wore black ones.
As for its *ruí* (streamers),
I have never heard of it.
Nowadays, they cap with money,
which is also acceptable."
Yìzǐ said:
"The caps of the Three Kings,
how were they different?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The Zhōu *biàn*,
the Yīn *xǔ*,
the Xià *shōu*,
are all the same.
The Three Kings all shared the leather *biàn* with plain seams;
the *wěimào* was the way of Zhōu;
the *zhāngfǔ* was the way of Yīn;
the *wú zhuī* was the way of the Xià rulers."
Temple Regulations, Chapter Thirty-four
Wèi Jiāngjūn Wénzi was about to establish the temple of the late lord in his home,
and sent Zǐ Gāo to inquire of Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A public temple established in a private home
is not something found in ancient rites;
I do not know about it."
Zǐ Gāo said:
"May I ask about the system for establishing temples according to rank and status;
might I be permitted to hear about it?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The world has a king,
who divides the land and establishes states,
and sets up ancestral temples,
which determines the number of close or distant relatives, noble or lowly, many or few.
Therefore, the Son of Heaven establishes seven temples,
three Zhāo and three Mù,
and with the temple of the Great Ancestor, there are seven.
The temples of the Great Ancestor and those closest to it
are all sacrificed to monthly;
distant temples become tiāo-temples,
and there are two tiāo-temples,
where xiǎng and cháng sacrifices are performed and then they cease.
The feudal lords establish five temples,
two Zhāo and two Mù,
and with the temple of the Great Ancestor, there are five.
In the ancestral and paternal temples,
xiǎng and cháng sacrifices are performed and then they cease.
A high official establishes three ancestral temples,
one in the zhāo order and one in the mù order,
together with the temple of the grand ancestor, making three.
The offerings and regular sacrifices then cease.
A scholar establishes one ancestral temple,
called the "father's temple."
If the grandfather has no temple,
they are combined, and the offerings and regular sacrifices then cease.
Commoners have no ancestral temple;
they perform the four seasonal sacrifices in their sleeping quarters.
This is what has not changed from the time of Yǒu Yú to the Zhōu dynasty.
In general, what the emperors of the four dynasties called "suburban sacrifices"
were all to match Heaven;
what they called "dì sacrifices"
were all inclusive of the grand five-year sacrifices.
Those who should be considered grand ancestors,
then their temples are not destroyed;
those who do not reach the level of grand ancestor,
even if they are included in the dì and suburban sacrifices,
their temples are destroyed.
In ancient times,
the ancestor had merit and the progenitor had virtue,
and those who were seen as both ancestors and progenitors,
their temples were not destroyed."
Zǐ Gāo asked, saying:
"The sacrificial classics say:
'The Yú clan took Zhuānxū as their ancestor and Yáo as their progenitor;
the Xià dynasty also took Zhuānxū as their ancestor and Yǔ as their progenitor;
the Yīn people took Qì as their ancestor and Tāng as their progenitor;
the Zhōu people took Wén Wáng as their ancestor and Wǔ Wáng as their progenitor.'
These four ancestors and four progenitors,
are sometimes from different eras.
or whose deceased ancestors had meritorious achievements,
their temples are permissible.
If Yú (虞) reveres Yáo (堯) as its progenitor,
and Xià (夏) takes Zhuānxū (顓頊) as its ancestor,
both being meritorious figures from different dynasties,
is it also permissible to maintain their temples? 」
Confucius said:
"Excellent,
your question is well-posed.
Like the ancestors and progenitors of Yin and Zhou,
their temples should not be destroyed.
As for other ancestors and progenitors,
whose merits and virtues are not inferior,
even if they belong to different dynasties,
there should be no doubt in venerating them.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
'Dense is the shade of the sweet pear tree,
do not prune it, do not cut it down.'
Where Shào Bó (邵伯) rested,
the Zhōu people's attitude toward Shào Gōng (邵公),
loving the man,
they even respected the tree where he stayed.
How much more so should we not respect and venerate the temples of our ancestors, given their merit and virtue?"

King Wǔ conquered Yin and reversed the policies of Shang.

Suburban sacrifices were made to Hòu Jì,
and the people knew to honor their fathers.
Sacrifices were made in the Mingtang,
and the people knew about filial piety.
Audiences were held,
and then the lords knew how to be subjects.
Royal plowing was performed,
and then the people knew how to respect their parents.
These six are the great teachings of the world.
Feeding the Three Elders and Five Experienced Ones in the Great Learning,
the Son of Heaven bared his shoulder and cut the sacrificial animal,
held the sauce and offered it,
held the goblet and rinsed it,
wore the crown and controlled the shield and axe,
in order to teach the younger brothers of the lords.
In this way,
the ways of the Zhōu dynasty would extend in all directions,
and rites and music would intercommunicate.

Wèn Yù Dì Sānshíliù Asking About Jade, Chapter Thirty-Six
Zǐgòng wèn yú Kǒngzǐ yuē: Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
「Gǎn wèn jūnzǐ yù guì ér mín jiàn, "May I ask, why is it that gentlemen value jade and despise common stones?
hé yě? What is the reason?
Wèi yù zhī guǎ ér mín zhī duō yú? 」 Is it because jade is scarce and common stones are plentiful?"
Kǒngzǐ yuē: Kǒngzǐ said:
「Fēi wèi yù zhī guǎ gù guì zhī yě, "It is not because jade is scarce that it is valued,
mín zhī duō gù jiàn zhī yě, nor because common stones are plentiful that they are despised.
Fú xīzhě jūnzǐ bǐ dé yú yù yān: Indeed, in the past, gentlemen compared virtues to jade:
wēnrùn ér zé, Being warm and moist,
rén yě; is benevolence;
zhěnmì yǐ lì, Being dense and firm,
zhì yě; is wisdom;
lián ér bù guì, Being honest but not sharp,
yì yě; is righteousness;
chuí zhī rú zhuì, Hanging down like a pendant,
lǐ yě; is propriety;
kòu zhī, When struck,
qí shēng qīngyuè ér cháng, its sound is clear, resonant, and lingering,
qí zhōng zé chù rán, and its end is abrupt,
yuè yě; is music;
xiá bù yǎn yú, A flaw does not conceal its beauty,
yú bù yǎn xiá, nor does its beauty conceal a flaw,
zhōng yě; is loyalty;
To be trustworthy and reaching far and wide is
trustworthiness;
Qi like a white rainbow is
Heaven;
spirit manifest in mountains and rivers is
Earth;
jade emblems distinctly displayed is
virtue;
what everyone under Heaven values is
the Dao.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"Speaking of this gentleman,
his warmth is like jade."
Therefore, the gentleman values it."
Confucius said:
"Enter his state,
and its teachings can be known:
His people,
gentle and kind,
are taught by the *Book of Poetry*;
being perceptive and understanding the distant,
are taught by the *Book of Documents*;
broad-minded, easy-going and good,
are taught by the *Book of Music*;
pure, tranquil, subtle and profound,
are taught by the *Book of Changes*;
Gōng, jiǎn, zhuāng, jìng (恭儉莊敬),
is the teaching of the *Lǐ* (《禮》);
shǔ cí bǐ shì (屬辭比事),
is the teaching of the *Chūnqiū* (《春秋》).
Therefore, the fault of the *Shī* (《詩》) is foolishness;
the fault of the *Shū* (《書》) is falseness.
The fault of the *Yuè* (《樂》) is extravagance;
the fault of the *Yì* (《易》) is treachery;
the fault of the *Lǐ* (《禮》) is tediousness;
the fault of the *Chūnqiū* (《春秋》) is disorder.
If one is gentle and sincere without being foolish,
then he is deeply versed in the *Shī* (《詩》);
if one is knowledgeable and insightful without being false,
then he is deeply versed in the *Shū* (《書》);
if one is broad-minded and agreeable without being extravagant,
then he is deeply versed in the *Yuè* (《樂》);
if one is pure, tranquil, refined, and subtle without being treacherous,
then he is deeply versed in the *Yì* (《易》);
if one is respectful, frugal, solemn, and reverent without being tedious,
then he is deeply versed in the *Lǐ* (《禮》);
if one uses words and relates events without disorder,
then he is deeply versed in the *Chūnqiū* (《春秋》).
Heaven has four seasons:
spring, summer, autumn, winter;
wind, rain, frost, and dew;
none of these is without teaching.
The earth bears spiritual influences,
inhaling and exhaling thunder;
The myriad forms and countless things,
are all nothing other than instruction.
Clear understanding resides within oneself,
one's spirit and will are like the divine.
When something is about to arrive,
its signs must appear beforehand.
Therefore, the teachings of Heaven and Earth
are aligned with those of the sages.
It is said in the *Book of Poetry*:
'Mount Sōng is the great peak,
its steepness reaches the sky.
This peak sends down spirits,
giving birth to Fǔ and Shēn.
Because of Shēn and Fǔ,
they are the bulwark of Zhōu.
The four states flourish,
and proclaim it in all directions.'
This is the virtue of (King) Wén and (King) Wǔ.
Displaying his civil virtue,
harmonizing these four states,
this is the virtue of King Wén.
All the kings of the Three Dynasties,
must first seek their good repute.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
'Bright and clear is the Son of Heaven,
his good repute never ceases.'
This is the virtue of the Three Dynasties."
Zǐ Zhāng asked about what the sage uses to teach.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shī!
I'll tell you.
The sage is enlightened in ritual and music,
he simply puts them into practice."
Zǐ Zhāng asked again.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Shī,
do you think it necessarily involves setting out tables and mats,
bowing and yielding, ascending and descending,
offering, presenting, responding, and returning toasts,
and only then can it be called ritual?
Do you think it necessarily involves performing aligned formations,
holding feather plumes and flutes,
playing bells and drums,
and only then can it be called music?
Words that can be carried out are
ritual;
actions that can be enjoyed are
music.
The sage practices these two,
in order to cultivate himself and face south (to govern).
Therefore, the world is at peace,
the people are obedient and submissive,
the officials carry out their duties,
and those above and below have ritual propriety.
